articles.title: UK bookmakers that warned over illicit market had deal with offshore casinos
articles.summary:
Content provider part-owned by Ladbrokes, William Hill and Betfred owner signed deal with Santeda network, Casino Secrets leak reveals

Three UK bookmakers that have repeatedly warned of the…

blocks.text: Three UK bookmakers that have repeatedly warned of the dangers of the illicit market have also benefited from a lucrative deal with one of the world’s largest offshore casinos, the Guardian can reveal.

Details of the arrangement emerged as a result of last week’s Casino Secrets leak, which saw the release of thousands of confidential files held by the gambling regulator on the Caribbean island of Curaçao, a haven for offshore betting sites.
One leaked file concerns the Santeda online casino network, which has been accused of illegally targeting vulnerable gamblers in the UK and has been fined in Spain for operating without a licence.

The file shows that Santeda signed a deal in 2022 with Sports Information Services (SIS) – a UK-based gambling content provider part-owned by Ladbrokes, William Hill and Fred Done, the billionaire owner of Betfred.

The three bookmakers have repeatedly warned the government that excessive regulation or taxation could drive their customers into the arms of rogue offshore casinos with no licence to operate in Britain.
According to the leak, all three have also benefited from a share of tens of millions of pounds in dividends paid out by SIS after it signed the contract with Santeda.
The companies are understood to have been unaware of the deal at the time it was signed. Matt Zarb-Cousin, a prominent gambling reform campaigner, advised them to get their “house in order”.
The bookmakers collectively own more than 50% of SIS, which supplies gambling sites with live horse racing, greyhound and esports content, as well as data used to settle bets with customers.
The use of such data is critical to online betting companies, helping them serve customers and process their bets.
The leaked contract shows that SIS also agreed to provide Santeda websites with these services for two years, under a contract that auto-renewed unless either side opted to terminate it.
Under the terms of the deal, SIS received a percentage of revenues from losing bets placed via Santeda’s brands.
It is not clear whether the contract is still active, or how much SIS earned from it. SIS declined to say whether the deal had been terminated.

Industry sources said that Ladbrokes, William Hill and Fred Done could not have known about the deal with Santeda, owing to controls designed to prevent them accessing commercially-sensitive information about industry rivals.
One source said the companies were “furious” with SIS for doing business with Santeda, at a time when licensed operators were stepping up their warnings about the illicit market.

Entain said it was “not a party to the commercial or customer arrangements SIS decides to strike. Now that this relationship has come to light, we take it very seriously and have raised our concerns to SIS”.
The contract with Santeda does not permit the use of SIS data in the UK.

But it appears to show that SIS supplied information to multiple Santeda websites that a previous Guardian investigation found was illegally targeting UK customers, including via promotional material apparently aimed at people trying to quit.
Santeda’s Curaçao licence does not permit it to operate in most leading jurisdictions that regulate gambling, such as the UK and US.

Companies House filings suggest that SIS’s shareholders – including Ladbrokes, William Hill and Done – have received at least £37m in dividends since the deal with Santeda was signed, including £30m in 2023.
after newsletter promotion
Ladbrokes owns 23% of SIS, suggesting it has received £8.5m in payouts over the period.

Stella David, the chief executive of the Ladbrokes owner Entain, has criticised Premier League football clubs for “complicity” in fuelling illicit operators and warned that such firms could be boosted by any rise in taxes on licensed operators such as Ladbrokes.
William Hill appears to have received more than £7m from its near-20% stake in SIS.
Earlier this year, the bookmaker’s owner, Evoke, blamed the illicit market for weak online revenues.
Fred Done, who is also a director of SIS, holds an 8% stake, indicating his share of shareholder payouts was nearly £3m.

Done warned the chancellor this month that higher taxes on slot machines – under consideration as part of the upcoming budget – would drive punters to illicit market sites that don’t pay tax, contribute to horse racing or exercise regulatory controls.

Zarb-Cousin, the director of the gambling-blocking company Gamban and a longtime campaigner for tougher laws, said: “While the UK’s biggest gambling firms have been warning about the risks of growing the illicit market if the government increases tax and regulation, the very same firms are profiting from it.
“If the gambling industry is concerned about the black market, it needs to get its own house in order by cutting all ties with it.”
A spokesperson for SIS said all of its customers agreed to “only offer SIS products where it is legal to do so and where they have the necessary regulatory licences”.
They added: “Customers commit that they will comply with all such laws and licences at all times.
“Where SIS becomes aware that these terms are not being adhered to it takes corrective action to enforce the position, up to and including suspension or termination of contracts.”
The Guardian approached Evoke and Fred Done for comment.

articles.title: ‘It’s utter surrealism’: Venezuela’s Chavistas lament government’s embrace of Trump
articles.summary:
Diehard Hugo Chávez supporters struggle to comprehend ideological U-turn being executed by Delcy Rodríguez’s interim administration

He was one of the most passionate propagandists for Hugo…
articles.byline: Camille Rodríguez Montilla in Caracas and Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: He was one of the most passionate propagandists for Hugo Chávez’s Bolivarian revolution: a feisty leftist TV personality who spent more than two decades singing the movement’s praises on his state-funded show, The Razorblade.
Mario Silva’s devotion was such that he often hosted his programme with Chávez’s portrait behind him and he had El Comandante’s curly signature tattooed on to his left wrist.

But nine months after Venezuela’s political landscape was scrambled by Donald Trump’s abduction of Chávez’s heir, Nicolás Maduro, Silva’s show has been cancelled, and its host is livid about the revolution’s direction under Maduro’s former deputy, Delcy Rodríguez.

“[I feel] a lot of disappointment – depressed … and sometimes I wake up and feel like the world is collapsing around me,” the 66-year-old said during a rare interview at his home studio in the mountains outside the capital, Caracas.

Silva has spent recent weeks railing against Rodríguez’s interim administration on YouTube, his home since his programme on state TV was axed, berating those he blames for Venezuela’s “shameful and utterly illegitimate surrender” to the US.

Since January, a parade of high-ranking US officials – including the head of the CIA, the chair of the joint chiefs of staff and the energy secretary, Chris Wright – have visited Caracas, while Trump recently trumpeted striking “the biggest oil deal in world history” with Rodríguez’s regime. Last week, Rodríguez and Trump met on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, posing for a smiley photograph that left diehard Chavistas such as Silva aghast.

“I thought it [the photo] was artificial intelligence or something like that. But it’s surrealism, utter surrealism … It’s impossible to understand,” Silva fumed on YouTube as a red flag emblazoned with the faces of Karl Marx, Friedrich Engels and Vladimir Lenin hung behind him.

blocks.caption: Mario Silva in his home studio in La Guaira state, Venezuela. Photograph: Andrea Hernández Briceño/The Guardian

blocks.text: “They have surrendered this country and surrendered it the most vile and despicable way,” Silva went on. “Honestly, they are dragging the country’s name through the mud. They are dragging Chávez’s name through the mud.”

In another broadcast, Silva seethed about the cosy post-Maduro relationship that has developed between one-time anti-imperialist flagbearers in Caracas and Trump officials: “Traitors and lackeys, you will have to answer for this!”

Silva is not the only Chavista loyalist struggling to comprehend the ideological U-turn being executed by Rodríguez, who was Maduro’s vice-president but has engineered a historic rapprochement with the US since his rendition on 3 January.

Elías Jaua, a vice-president and foreign minister under Chávez, is also up in arms, and claims the feeling is widely shared. “What I hear from comrades across the country is bewilderment, disagreement and indignation,” said Jaua, who believes Trump’s oil deal “amounts to an act of pillage against an entire nation”.

blocks.caption: Venezuela’s interior minister Diosdado Cabello addressing a crowd during a march in support of Delcy Rodríguez last week. Photograph: Diko Betancourt/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Juan Barreto, a former member of the ruling Socialist party (PSUV) and mayor of Caracas, said such an agreement would have been unimaginable when the Bolivarian revolution began after Chávez’s 1998 election. He said Chavistas, who had once vowed “Not a drop of oil to the empire if Venezuela is attacked!”, were now in effect saying: “All of the oil reserves [for the US], for as long as you want!”
“The current situation is one of tutelage,” Barreto said.

Rodríguez has defended the deal, claiming it will create more than $209bn (£158bn) in revenues that will help improve healthcare and education. “We are thinking of Venezuela’s future,” she said in a recent TV broadcast.

Héctor Rodríguez, another prominent Chavista politician, has sought to deflect criticism of Venezuela’s interim government by recalling how Chávez was forced to make a tactical retreat after his failed coup attempt in 1992. “No one can tell me Chávez was a coward. He understood that the balance of power had shifted … and decided to take a step backwards,” Rodríguez said recently.

​Last week as Delcy Rodríguez met Trump in New York, thousands of people ​joined a pro-government rall​y in Caracas, where supporters parroted the slogan “Delcy avanza, tú tienes mi confianza!” (“Move forward, Delcy. I trust in you!”).

blocks.caption: Ex National Assembly deputy and television presenter Mario Silva in his home studio. Photograph: Andrea Hernández Briceño/The Guardian

blocks.text: “No matter how much they kick and scream, there’s nothing they can do to try to cover up the success of President Delcy Rodríguez’s visit to New York,” her interior minister, Diosdado Cabello, ​told the crowd. Unlike at previous marches, there was scant mention of Maduro and few calls for him to be released.
The depth and potential consequences of Chavista anger over Rodríguez’s embrace of Venezuela’s longtime foes in Washington remain unclear.

Orlando Pérez, a Latin America expert from the University of North Texas at Dallas, recognised there was indignation at what some considered a sellout of their anti-imperialist ideals. “There are Chavistas that are pissed off, there’s no question about it,” he said. “There are Chavistas who see this as a betrayal of Hugo Chávez and the betrayal of the movement.”

But Pérez believed that for many Chavistas who had remained in power after Trump’s invasion, the “pragmatic reality” was that working with Washington was “a necessary evil” if it meant keeping Venezuela’s opposition out of power.

“If that means negotiating with Trump, if that means dealing with the CIA etc, it’s fine,” he said. “Beyond whatever ideological position they might have … I suspect most of them are gritting their teeth and just going along with this process as long as they can stay in power and keep their jobs. I think for most it’s as simple as that: it’s about their material wellbeing.”

However, Pérez believed Rodríguez’s government would need to demonstrate to supporters “tangible benefits to the cooperation” with the US in order to avoid a backlash. “They’re going to have to show that these things have a material consequence to the lives of their social base … if you don’t deliver, then it is going to get very volatile,” he warned.

blocks.caption: A Venezuelan government supporter carries dolls depicting Hugo Chávez and the pro-government comic-book characters Super Bigote and Cilita at a march in Caracas backing Delcy Rodríguez’s participation in the UN general assembly in New York. Photograph: Juan Barreto/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: So far there has been no sign of significant resistance from outraged supporters of Chavismo. But Silva claimed the government’s new direction and economic policies could eventually trigger a social uprising and protests.

“Worsening economic conditions will degrade [people’s] quality of life, and that pressure is bound to explode. It has to explode – it’s not just wishful thinking. This isn’t a prediction born of desire, it’s an inevitability,” said the broadcaster, who has claimed he is facing investigation for alleged acts of “aggravated defamation and slander against the interim government”.

Silva lit one cigarette after another as he recalled the early hours of 3 January 2026 when, as US troops swept into Venezuela’s capital, he realised the revolution he had spent more than 20 years defending was not going to defend itself.

The Chavista broadcaster said he moved from one strategic point to another across Caracas before finally calling the commander at his assigned post. “I said: ‘Hey, what happened? Where are the weapons?’” Silva recalled, his face settling into a sad grin as he remembered the answer. “Go to sleep, Mario,” he was told.
Silva pauses. “You have no idea how disappointed I was.”

articles.title: Vancouver band cancels Charlottetown show after venue denied transgender member washroom access
articles.summary: A Vancouver punk band that was set to play in Charlottetown this past weekend cancelled its show after a transgender band member was stopped from using the women's washroom at the venue.

image.caption: Vancouver band Rougaroux had a show scheduled at Sportsman's Club in Charlottetown on Sept. 27, but cancelled it after one of the musicians was denied access to a washroom. (Tony Davis/CBC)

blocks.text: PEI
A Vancouver punk band that was set to play in Charlottetown this past weekend cancelled its show after a transgender band member was stopped from using the women's washroom at the venue.
'The reality is hate is on the rise, and some of it relates to deep-rooted stuff'
Rougaroux was in Prince Edward Island as part of a cross-country tour and had a show planned at the Sportsman's Club.
Members of the band are transgender, including singer Marina Hanly, who — as equipment was being unloaded — needed to use the washroom.

"As I was just outside of the washroom … trying to mentally prepare to just go in there, the bartender came up and taped up a little handwritten paper sign outside the door that said 'ladies only,' and said, 'Hey, we're very strict about this,'" Hanly said.

Band member George Finley said he found Hanly to the side of the stage area and asked about what happened. He said he walked to the washroom and "ripped down the sign" before approaching the bar and asking for an explanation.

"The words I used were, 'Why, when my female fiancé is going to use the washroom, did you feel the need to walk in front of her and put this sign up?' [The bartender] responded with, like, 'Well, if she's female, there should be no problem,'" Finley said.
"There are four trans women travelling with us, including Marina, and I myself am a trans man. So I walked over there and I told everyone to get the gear and get out, that we were leaving."

items: 'Queer people exist and always have': Why organizers say Pride still matters on P.E.I.
Researchers hope to include Islanders' voices in their study on gender-affirming care

blocks.text: The manager of Sportsman's Club told CBC News that the business tries to accommodate transgender people, but that doesn't include access to washrooms and the venue does not have gender-neutral facilities.
The manager said there are no plans to change the bathroom policy.
Derrick Biso was set to perform at the show as their drag persona, Remedy, after hearing the show was coming to town and reaching out to the band.
"[It's] certainly a really disappointing experience, very discouraging and certainly one that is a violation of people's human rights to access washrooms," Biso said.
"The reality is hate is on the rise, and some of it relates to deep-rooted stuff."
Hanly said Rougaroux doesn't hide who they are, and imagery is prominent on the band's social media.
"It's pretty clear that we are talking about queerness and that that is kind of like a big part of our identity as a band," she said.
"I had talked to them on the phone when I was booking this but, at the same time, you kind of would think that a venue would do … the bare minimum in looking at who they're booking."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Lucas McInnis is a journalist at CBC Prince Edward Island. He can be reached at lucas.mcinnis@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Sara Duterte trial recap, Oct. 1: Trillanes out, AMLC witness moved
articles.summary: The impeachment court on Thursday, October 1, lost most of what was slated to be a pivotal stretch of testimony.

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The impeachment court on Thursday, October 1, lost most of what was slated to be a pivotal stretch of testimony after prosecutors dropped former Sen. Antonio Trillanes IV and the anti-money laundering witness was moved to next week.
Prosecutors had lined up both witnesses for Thursday and Friday under Article II, which mainly accuses Vice President Sara Duterte of unexplained wealth and failing to divest from business interests.

After much ado, it turns out Trillanes would not be taking the stand after all. Lead prosecutor Rep. Jinky Luistro told the court today that the panel "has finally decided not to present" the former senator.

That came two days after prosecutors sought to put him on the stand ahead of their other witnesses, and a day after House prosecutor Rep. Terry Ridon said Trillanes's testimony would reveal weighty matters that "go beyond" the vice president's bank accounts.
The court also granted the defense's request to postpone the presentation of AMLC Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura to Monday so it could have more time to prepare.
In the end, a day meant for a full slate of hearings produced testimony from just two witnesses, the registers of deeds of Davao City and Samal.

They identified land titles, deeds of sale and tax declarations for properties registered to Carpio. Both said repeatedly that their role is ministerial and that they could not say whether the properties matched entries in Duterte's SALNs.
Here are the three highlights from today's proceedings.
1. 'Belated final position': Prosecution drops Trillanes
Luistro announced the decision to skip Trillanes while submitting the prosecution's revised order of witnesses.
"We seek the kind indulgence of the honorable impeachment court for the belated final position on this particular concern," Luistro said, without giving a reason.

When lead defense counsel Sheila Sison asked whether Trillanes was being removed from the list for good or only deferred, Luistro said the prosecution "will no longer be presenting the former senator."

The move capped a week of back-and-forth over Trillanes. On Tuesday, the court declined to subpoena the former senator, saying bank records or an AMLC witness should come before him, though it said the prosecution could still call him voluntarily.
In an attempt to drum up excitement for Trillanes' presentation, the prosecution said in a Tuesday press briefing that the information Trillanes had in store for the court would "draw attention."
In April, Trillanes claimed before the House justice committee that Duterte and members of her immediate family received millions from an alleged drug lord. Duterte has denied the allegation.
Trillanes released a statement today clarifying that the decision to drop him from the witness list was made at his request.

“Earlier in the day, I requested the House prosecution under Chair Jinky Luistro to formally withdraw my name as a witness for the prosecution. This way, the prosecution panel would be relieved from the pressure it is going through,” Trillanes said in a statement.
The former senator is scheduled to give a press conference tomorrow at Club Filipino in Manila, where he is expected to present to the media his allegations against the vice president.
2. AMLC testimony pushed to Monday
After a brief break mid-afternoon, the defense asked the court to defer the presentation of the AMLC witness.
The prosecution's case on Article II rests largely on AMLC reports covering P6.77 billion in transactions involving the vice president and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio.

Sison argued that they only received the 11-page AMLC summary late in the morning Thursday. She said this left them not enough time to examine the "at least 23 to 24 boxes of documents" contained in the summary.
In addition to the volume of documents, the defense also raised a concern about the documents' confidentiality, citing Section 8-A of the Anti-Money Laundering Act.

In opposition, House prosecutor Rep. Chel Diokno argued that the defense had notice of the AMLC records since September 2 and pointed to the court's July 20, 2026 ruling issuing a subpoena for the AMLC records.
That ruling, Diokno said, affirmed that Section 8-A regulates unauthorized internal leaks by AMLC personnel but does not nullify the Senate's subpoena powers as an impeachment court.

Sen. Tito Sotto and Sen. Risa Hontiveros both expressed reservations with the defense's argument to hold off on the AMLC presentation due to confidentiality concerns. Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano argued that adherence to procedural fairness justified granting the defense a brief extension.
Escudero, in the end, citing courtesy and equity, granted the deferment and rescheduled the AMLC witness presentation to Monday.
This will be followed by the presentation of witnesses from banks and insurance companies and the Bureau of Internal Revenue.
3. Raffy Tulfo calls out the prosecution's witness choices
Before the prosecution announced its decision to drop Trillanes, Sen. Raffy Tulfo made a manifestation early in the proceedings today to seemingly chastise the prosecution for its recent showing.
Upon learning that the prosecution had yet to present Trillanes, Tulfo criticized the prosecution's handling and order of presentation of witnesses.
"'Yung prosecution minsan pumapalpak palpak," he said. "There are times na naglalagay kayo ng mga witnesses dito na hindi naman kailangan talaga."
(The prosecution sometimes messes up... There are times when you present witnesses here who aren't really necessary.)
Tulfo said he has observed some senators "looking sleepy" and repeatedly dashing off for a bathroom break.
The prosecution said it would "take due notice and consider the advice of the senator judge."

articles.title: Sandiganbayan finds ex-DSWD exec guilty of graft, malversation over PDAF misuse
articles.summary: The Sandiganbayan on Thursday sentenced a former regional director of the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) to more than 20 years of imprisonment for graft and malversation over…

blocks.text: Published October 1, 2026 4:53pm

The Sandiganbayan on Thursday sentenced a former regional director of the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) to more than 20 years of imprisonment for graft and malversation over alleged misuse of a lawmaker’s pork barrel allocation.
In an 88-page ruling, the anti-graft court's Fifth Division meted Honorita Bayudan six years to ten years of imprisonment for graft as well as 14 years to 18 years for malversation.
She was perpetually disqualified from public office.
It ordered her to pay a fine of P5 million, representing the amount malversed, and another P5 million to the government with an interest rate of 6% per annum until finality of the decision.
“The court acknowledges the plight of the accused who may be bearing the consequences not only of her acts but also that of her subordinates,” it said.

“Nonetheless, the laws under which the accused was charged are clear. ‘Dura lex sed lex.’ The law may be harsh but that is the law. This court has therefore no other option but to apply the same,” it added.

The case stemmed from the alleged irregularities in the Priority Development Assistance Fund (PDAF) allocation of Congresswoman Consuelo Dy for the first tranche of Fiscal Year 2007 in the amount of P8 million.
The budget was for the Comprehensive Integrated Delivery of Social Services (CIDSS) project to be implemented by the Department DSWD-National Capital Region.

According to the Sandiganbayan, the DSWD-NCR, then represented by Bayudan, Dy, and Unlad Pinoy Organization Inc. (UPOI) entered into a memorandum of agreement (MOA) for the implementation of the CIDSS.
In convicting Bayudan, the Sandiganbayan found that she acted with manifest partiality, evident bad faith, and/or gross inexcusable negligence.

The court noted that she was directly involved in the registration of UPOI as Social Welfare and Development Agency, the execution of the MOA, the transfer of funds, and the implementation and monitoring of the project.

“In this entire process, the court found accused Bayudan to have committed glaring irregularities that reflect manifest partiality and evident bad faith on her part, or at the very least, gross inexcusable negligence,” it said.
The Sandiganbayan found that the release of funds to UPOI was not in accordance with a Commission on Audit circular and the MOA.
“Despite this, accused Bayudan allowed it to happen,” it said.

According to the court, the MOA presented to Bayudan did not bear the names and signatures of the individuals required to sign it. The MOA was also undated and unnotarized, contrary to the PDAF Utilization and Management Workflow.
It said that it was incumbent for Bayudan to refer the MOA back to the Standards Unit if she found any irregularity in its execution.
Aside from this, the Sandiganbayan flagged the DSWD-NCR’s release of P5 million to UPOI on March 29, 2007, even though the total budget was supposed to be released in two tranches.
The Sandiganbayan also said that Bayudan failed to monitor the implementation of the project or to ensure its monitoring.
“Nonetheless, accused Bayudan failed to do so. She chose to leave UPOI free from scrutiny and did not actively perform her duties under the MOA and as Regional Director of DSWD-NCR,” it said.

“Without a doubt, these acts show that accused Bayudan's negligence is not merely simple but gross and inexcusable, considering her position and the circumstances mentioned above,” it added.—AOL, GMA News

articles.title: SC junks petition questioning session that ousted Cayetano as Senate president
articles.summary: 'The Court resolved to dismiss the Petition for Certiorari for failure to show sufficiently that the respondents committed grave abuse of discretion in holding a session on June 3, 2026,' the SC says

items: The Supreme Court dismissed a petition challenging the Senate's June 3, 2026 session, where Senator Sherwin Gatchalian was elected Senate president pro tempore.
The Court found no evidence of grave abuse of discretion by the Senate majority in holding the session, which was deemed in accordance with applicable law.
The session was significant as it allowed the Senate minority to reach a quorum and declare all positions vacant, leading to Gatchalian's election as Senate president.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Supreme Court (SC) junked a petition questioning the Senate’s June 3, 2026 session – the day when Senator Sherwin Gatchalian was elected Senate president pro tempore and Senator Alan Peter Cayetano was ousted as the upper chamber’s head.

“The Court resolved to dismiss the Petition for Certiorari for failure to show sufficiently that the respondents committed grave abuse of discretion in holding a session on June 3, 2026, which, on the contrary, appear to be in accord with the facts and applicable law and jurisprudence,” the SC said based on a document posted by Senator Kiko Pangilinan.

𝗕𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗞𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗡𝗘𝗪𝗦𝗦𝗖, 𝗗𝗜𝗡𝗜𝗦𝗠𝗜𝗦 𝗔𝗡𝗚 𝗣𝗘𝗧𝗜𝗦𝗬𝗢𝗡 𝗟𝗔𝗕𝗔𝗡 𝗦𝗔 𝗝𝗨𝗡𝗘 𝟯 𝗦𝗘𝗡𝗔𝗧𝗘 𝗦𝗘𝗦𝗦𝗜𝗢𝗡Sa resolution na may petsang August 26, 2026, ibinasura ng Korte ang petition for certiorari na inihain nina Atty. Valeriano S. Loon at Atty. Zigfred… pic.twitter.com/SXAZKUG4xT— Kiko Pangilinan (@kikopangilinan) October 1, 2026

In their petition docketed as GR No. E-07032, lawyers Valeriano Loon and Zigfred Diaz filed the certiorari petition against the current Senate majority members questioning the June 3 session. Certiorari is a legal action filed to seek a review of another body’s decision or to seek grave abuse of discretion.
The SC’s resolution is dated August 26, but was made public on Thursday, October 1.
The then-Senate majority led by Cayetano skipped sessions to avoid reaching a quorum of 12 – or the minimum number of senators present to do official business. This rendered the Senate paralyzed.
But, on June 3, the then-minority finally reached a quorum when Senator Chiz Escudero, now impeachment presiding officer, appeared at the upper chamber to join the session.

Since a quorum had been reached, the senators present moved to declare all positions vacant and elected Gatchalian as Senate president pro tempore (in essence, acting Senate president), and the new chairpersons of committees. Gatchalian was later elected as Senate president.

blocks.caption: The Senate’s quorum of 12 senators is legal — here’s why

blocks.text: The minority’s basis was the 1949 Supreme Court (SC) case of Avelino v. Cuenco, where the High Court ruled that the quorum of 12, during a Senate session on February 21, 1949, was valid. In that ruling, the SC said that 12 was enough to reach a quorum because the available senators then were only 23, not 24.

Further, the SC said in the Avelino doctrine that the wording “majority of each House” in the 1987 Constitution to reach a quorum did not mean “all” the members. So by computing the required number to reach a quorum, the Senate looked into the number of available members, not all of its members.

Meanwhile, Cayetano had filed a similar petition with the SC on June 16, asking the High Court to recognize him as Senate president. The status of this petition, however, has not yet been clarified. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Tinio says part of PH debt going into 'pork barrel'; DBM calls claim inaccurate
articles.summary: ACT Teachers party-list Representative Antonio Tinio said Thursday part of the growing debt that the Philippines was incurring was going into a pork barrel, which the Department of Budget and…

blocks.text: ACT Teachers party-list Representative Antonio Tinio said Thursday part of the growing debt that the Philippines was incurring was going into a pork barrel, which the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) denied.

During a press briefing on Wednesday, Tinio said the country's debt has been growing since the COVID-19 pandemic, and has further increased during the term of President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr.

"Ang tanong, of course is, lumalaki nang lumalaki ang utang, saan naman napunta ito? Saan ginagamit? Ginagamit ang malaking bahagi sa budget to cover the budget deficit. Again, papalaki rin ang budget deficit sa ilalim ng Marcos Jr. administration. Saan ginagastos ang utang para pondohan ang budget deficit? Linalagay sa pork," Tinio said.

(The question, of course, is, our debt keeps growing and growing. So, where is it going? Where is it being used? A big part of the budget is being used to cover the budget deficit. Again, the budget deficit under the Marcos Jr. administration is growing. Where is the borrowed money going to fund the deficit? It is being put in pork.)

Tinio said that P1.7 trillion of the budget deficit is being used in the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), infrastructure, flood control projects, farm-to-market-roads, and the Local Government Support Fund (LGSF).

The congressman cited the City of Naga and the City of Manila as areas where the LGSF was put into good use. He said it bankrolled repairs for the Jesse M. Robredo Coliseum in Naga, and funded the Senior Citizens Park and a community Pet Park in Manila.
However, the funds being discretionary raised an issue in other areas, Tinio said, with some poorer localities getting left behind.

Tinio also flagged the massive increase to ayuda programs such as the Department of Social Welfare and Development's Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situation, the Department of Health's Medical Assistance to Indigent and Financially Incapacitated Patients, and the Department of Labor and Employment's Tulong Panghanapbuhay sa Ating Disadvantaged/Displaced Workers.
"Pinalaki 'yung bahagi ng social services na pork barrel na dinadaan sa politiko na kailangan lumapit ka sa politiko para maka-access ka ng social services," Tinio said.
(They increased the part of social services that has to go through politicians, that people have to ask these politicians for access to these social services.)

In a separate report from the ACT Teachers party-list, the group said that as debt grew, so did the budget deficit. While the debt and the budget deficit grew, so did several government programs. However, the group said in the report that the figures merely compared amounts, and that "they don't trace particular loans to particular projects."
Conflated statements?
In a message to GMA News Online, DBM Undersecretary Goddes Hope Libiran said Tinio's statement conflated separated statements.
According to Libiran, government borrowing finances the overall fiscal deficit, or the gap between government revenue and spending.

"It does not follow that borrowed funds are being placed in or used for so-called 'pork.' More importantly, there is no appropriation identified as 'pork barrel' in the proposed FY 2027 National Expenditure Program," Libiran said.
The DBM spokesperson maintained that the P7.2-trillion National Expenditure Program clearly identified where the government resources will go.

"It is therefore inaccurate to draw a direct line from government borrowing, to the fiscal deficit, and then to alleged 'pork.' Borrowing, deficit financing, and specific appropriations under the national budget are distinct fiscal concepts," Libiran said.
The DBM executive also defended the LGSF, saying that it was not pork either. She said it was not an unrestricted fund for political patronage.
"There are already clear statutory, administrative, and accountability safeguards governing the allocation, release, and utilization of the LGSF," Libiran said.

"For the LGSF-Financial Assistance to LGUs in particular, the process is not based on the intervention or endorsement of political intermediaries. Requests originate from the LGUs themselves, based on their identified local needs and priorities," Libiran said.

These requests are also not guaranteed, as the DBM has criteria that considered several factors before they were approved. Libiran also cited Belgica v. Secretary of Budget and Management, which ruled that the LGSF is a valid appropriation.
"The LGSF does not give the Executive—or any individual official—unfettered discretion to decide where public funds will go," she said.
GMA News Online has also reached out to Malacañang for a statement, but it has yet to respond as of posting time. — VDV, GMA News

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

WASHINGTON, USA – An artificial intelligence research firm said on Wednesday, September 30, that AI agents tried to hack into a Canadian government website, casting the effort a failed hacking attempt, while Canada said there were no indications its systems were compromised.

AI research firm Transluce said the attempts exhibited tactics “consistent with prior observed agent activity that we have attributed to OpenAI in a similar timeframe.” But it added that it was not confidently attributing these attempts to OpenAI.
The agents attempted to access Library and Archives Canada on May 28 and June 9, Transluce said in a blog post. Transluce said it disclosed the action to the Canadian government on Monday.

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security said on Tuesday it was aware of reports of suspected AI agent activity. “There is no indication that government systems have been compromised at this time,” it said in a statement.

“We do not confidently attribute these attempts to OpenAI, but they exhibit tactics consistent with prior observed agent activity that we have attributed to OpenAI in a similar timeframe,” Transluce said.

OpenAI said it was “aware of reports of OpenAI models attempting to access publicly available information from Canadian government websites.” A spokesperson said OpenAI was reviewing the reported findings and had provided an initial briefing to Canadian officials conducting the government’s review.

The ​world’s leading AI companies have warned ⁠of the risks posed by AI to ​humanity, appealing for governments to work together to ​manage the increasingly powerful technology. Governments around the world have struggled to keep pace with rapid advances in AI.

Free online service arquivo.pt, the national Portuguese web archive that is operated by the Portuguese Foundation for Science and Technology, captured 899 requests hitting the “collection-search” service of the Library and Archives Canada, including a series of apparently failed rudimentary hacking attempts, on May 28 and June 9, Transluce said.
Several recent breaches globally by rogue AI agents have alarmed governments and companies.

Last week, Australia said an OpenAI agent breached a government health data portal in June, gaining unauthorized access to files, in ​what was the first known instance of an AI agent hacking into a government website.
OpenAI apologized on Tuesday for the hacking of the Australian government website by the rogue AI agent. – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘Politics can be brutal’: Sarah Hanson-Young speaks out about divisions within Greens
articles.summary:
Greens sources say the relationship between new leader David Shoebridge and runner-up Mehreen Faruqi is seriously strained

  • Get our

blocks.text: Sarah Hanson-Young has spoken out about major divisions in the Greens party room, offering support to newly elected leader David Shoebridge and describing politics as “brutal”.
The South Australian senator contested Wednesday’s leadership ballot, finishing behind Shoebridge and outgoing deputy leader, Mehreen Faruqi.
Former leader Larissa Waters shocked colleagues by resigning on Monday, over serious health concerns.
Hanson-Young was eliminated after the first ballot with only two votes.
“God, politics can be brutal,” she said in a video posted to social media, after a bush walk with her husband on Thursday.
“Friendships made and lost, but it takes all types. We all care so deeply about the future of this country and the future of the planet.”
Hanson-Young said it would take a huge effort to defeat One Nation and its leader, Pauline Hanson, and warned “the radical right” would wreck the country if it wins power.
“Australians deserve a optimistic, caring, and defiant progressive force, and I won’t be backing down,” she said.
“I’m sorry we couldn’t pull it off this time, but buckle up, because we’ve got a lot of work to do.”
Her comments come a day after Faruqi criticised her colleagues for electing Shoebridge and demanded the party’s rank-and-file members be given a say in future leadership elections.
Greens sources say Shoebridge and Faruqi’s working relationship is seriously strained.

The New South Wales senator said she planned to pursue bold politics and radical action to fight “against genocide, wars, surging fascism” and climate change, working from outside “the constraints of the leadership team”.

In an interview with Guardian Australia’s Australian Politics podcast on Thursday, Shoebridge said he and the newly elected deputy, Victorian senator Steph Hodgins-May, had received a strong endorsement from their colleagues.
Shoebridge said he could work with Faruqi, praising her for effective community engagement.

“I have huge respect for Mehreen and the work that she does. And, acknowledging as well, the attacks that she gets and the way she keeps turning up proudly and strongly, taking the case forward in the face of all of those attacks.
“That is something that I have immense respect for and gratitude for.”
Shoebridge said Greens MPs wanted Faruqi to continue her engagement with voters and Greens members.
“Sometimes you want to be part of the leadership team. Sometimes you want to be out connecting with the community in a different way.
“We’re all human beings and we all know how in the moment how we can best contribute to the project.

“I take Maureen at her word that that’s how she thinks she can best connect with the community, how she can best connect with the project. And she has my 100% support to go on being the amazing Greens senator that we’ve all seen.”
He committed to giving rank and file party members the right to vote in leadership elections in time for the next scheduled contest, due to take place immediately after the next federal election.
A party plebiscite in 2020 saw 62% of Greens members support a party-wide vote for leader, but the move fell short of a required two-thirds majority.

articles.title: Cristiano Ronaldo walks out of Portugal camp
articles.summary: Cristiano Ronaldo has left Portugal’s camp after learning that he would not start the next Nations League match. Portugal's coach has denied reports of a rift between himself and the star player.

image.caption: Cristiano Ronaldo has seen limited action for Portugal during this international breakImage: Grzegorz Wajda/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: The 41-year-old forward left the Portugal camp on Wednesday after coach Jorge Jesus had told reporters at the Matchday-1 press conference that Cristiano Ronaldo would not feature in the starting lineup against Denmark in the Nations League.
The move comes amid reports of a rift between the Al-Nassr player and coach, something that Jesus denied.
The 72-year-old coach conceded that his captain had been disappointed to remain on the bench in Portugal's win over Norway on Sunday, but he insisted that there had been "no incident whatsoever."
Ronaldo didn't explain why he had taken the decision, but in an Instagram post he said that "in time" he would "tell the Portuguese people the truth about the reasons" behind his departure.

"Following the national team coach's news conference, and after a conversation with the president of the Portuguese football federation, I decided to leave the national team's training camp," he said, adding that he had always "dedicated" himself to the national team.
"Now is the time to wish good luck to Portugal and to all my teammates, without exception."

For its part, the Portuguese federation (FPF) confirmed that the five-time Ballon d'Or winner had left the camp and that the team's preparations for Thursday's match in Copenhagen would continue without him.
"The entire delegation remains fully focused on the national team's upcoming fixtures and on achieving our goals," it said.
It wasn't immediately clear whether Ronaldo's departure would extend beyond the current international break.

blocks.caption: Portugal coach Jorge Jesus has denied reports of a rift between himself and Cristiano RonaldoImage: Kristian Tuxen Ladegaard Berg/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: In Wednesday's press conference, Jesus had said that Ronaldo would start on the bench and may be brought on as a sub.
"I don't know what's going to happen in the game," the coach said.
"If we need him to play, he'll play. If not, he won't."
Limited action

Ronaldo started Portugal's 1-0 win over Wales last Thursday but was substituted in the 67th minute. He was on the bench but saw no action in Sunday's 2-1 win over Norway in Oslo. Portugal face Norway again at home this coming Sunday.
Portugal leads Group A4 of the Nations League with six points from two matches, three points more than Denmark and Norway.

Wednesday's news comes with Ronaldo's long-time rival Lionel Messi set to play his last match for Argentina next week. Earlier this year, Ronaldo, who is the all-time top goal scorer in men's competitive matches (979), had said recently that this Saudi Pro League season is likely to be the last of his professional career.
Earlier this year, he had said the 2026 World Cup would be the last of his career but did not say exactly when he would retire from international football.

articles.title: Badenoch proposes welfare reform that would stop many jobless under-25s getting universal credit – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Tories suggest ‘tough love’ approach amid issue of one million young people not in employment, education or training

Good morning. The Conservatives start their conference at the weekend and…

blocks.text: Good morning. The Conservatives start their conference at the weekend and Kemi Badenoch is kicking off proceedings by announcing a significant plan for welfare reform – stopping many under-25s from being able to claim universal credit, the main unemployment benefit.

Instead, they would get a new Get to Work Allowance – which would be subject to conditions from day one intended to help people find work. If after six months they are still out of work, they would go on to a new benefit, a Subsistence Allowance, worth just 70% of their previous claims.
The plans don’t relate to disability benefits, because they would only apply to people able to work.
Explaining the plans in an interview with the Spectator, Kemi Badenoch said:

double quotation markIt’s unfair to the people who get up and go to work, having others earn more than them for not working. Even families on benefits know that the system is out of control. But no one wants to be the one to get off the treadmill first. We need to force that. Government has to do that.

The Tories are describing this as a “tough love” approach designed to deal with the problem of around one million young people being Neets (not in employment, education or training). Tim Shipman, who interviewed Badenoch for the Spectator, has a more colourful description. “This is the nanny state with menaces; Mary Poppins with an umbrella gun,” he says.
And here is the party’s explanation of its plans from its news release.

double quotation markThe Conservatives will require all 18-24 year olds who attempt to claim universal credit and who have not previously worked for a continuous period of 6 months to participate in a Get to Work scheme in exchange for welfare. Participants will receive a new ‘Get to Work Allowance’ which is contingent on their participation in the scheme. To be exempt from these requirements 18-24 year olds will have to demonstrate that they have previously been in continuous employment for a period of 6 months or more, for a minimum of 16 hours a week. Young people on UC who are not subject to work-related requirements, such as for health reasons or due to caring responsibilities, will be exempt. The programme would last up to six months. Participants could leave earlier if they secure a job, apprenticeship or qualifying education or training place. For participants in the Get to Work Scheme, the new Get to Work Allowance will replace the universal credit standard allowance. After 6 months, if participants on the scheme have not entered work they will automatically move down to the new Subsistence Allowance announced last week by the Conservatives. This is paid at 70% of the current Standard Allowance and will be pre-loaded onto a Back to Work card that prevents claimants spending on alcohol, cigarettes and gambling. After six months they would continue to be subject to demanding conditions.

We have not heard from Labour yet, and that may be because the party is not sure yet how to respond. Alan Milburn, the former cabinet minister, has finished the final report from his inquiry into Neets and it is due to be published before the budget. He is also expected to propose measures that would impose more conditions on young people getting out-of-work benefits because he also wants to stop people being consigned to a life on benefits. And ministers are expected to adopt his plans. We don’t know the details of the Milburn/government scheme, and it will probably involve more carrot than stick than the Tory one. But there may well be quite a lot of overlap too.
I will post more on the plans, and the Badenoch interview, soon.

Parliament is not sitting, and there is not much in the Westminster diary. But Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, does have a rally at 2pm this afternoon where he will respond to Andy Burnham’s conference speech..

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: Prosecutor surprised Trillanes won't be presented as witness in impeachment trial
articles.summary: Prosecution panel member Bukidnon Rep. Keith Flores said he was surprised by the announcement of lead prosecutor Batangas Rep. Gerville Luistro that the prosecution would no longer present former…

blocks.text: Published October 1, 2026 4:19pm

Prosecution panel member Bukidnon Rep. Keith Flores said he was surprised by the announcement of lead prosecutor Batangas Rep. Gerville Luistro that the prosecution would no longer present former Sen. Antonio Trillanes IV as a witness in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Trillanes is supposed to testify in the article of impeachment involving alleged unexplained wealth of the Vice President.
“I was really surprised. I was preparing for the witnesses this morning; I was focused on that,” Flores said.
He was referring to his direct examination of Atty. Kathy Florence Baldonado of the Davao City Register of Deeds and Atty. Marcio Pineda of the Samal Register of Deeds.

The witnesses testified on pieces of property worth P6 million and P3 million, acquired by Duterte's husband, Atty. Manases Carpio. These were said to be unlisted in the Vice President's joint Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth with Carpio.
“I’m really sorry about former Senator Trillanes; I cannot answer that,” Flores said.
Asked if other House prosecutors were also surprised by Luistro’s announcement, Flores replied, “I really cannot say.”
In a statement issued later in the day, Trillanes said he asked Luistro to drop him from the roster of witnesses so as not to burden the prosecution. –NB, GMA News

items: The National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) has agreed to stop contesting permit and regulatory fees imposed by the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC), settling years of litigation.
A compromise agreement was signed on October 1, recognizing the fees as regulatory and ensuring that past payments satisfy NGCP's obligations.
The agreement will be submitted to the Supreme Court and Court of Appeals for approval, with the ERC emphasizing the importance of clarity and public benefit from the fees.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) has agreed to stop contesting permit and regulatory fees imposed by the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC), settling years of litigation over whether the grid operator’s franchise exempts it from the charges.
The ERC and NGCP signed a compromise agreement on Thursday, October 1, covering disputes over permit fees imposed on individual transmission projects and annual supervision and regulation fees.

NGCP had consistently paid the charges under protest while challenging them before the Court of Appeals and Supreme Court. The grid operator argued that its congressional franchise exempted it from the fees, while the ERC maintained that the charges were regulatory and administrative in nature rather than taxes.

Under the settlement, NGCP recognizes the permit and supervision and regulation charges as regulatory fees imposed under the ERC’s mandate. It also agreed that it would no longer contest that characterization in the cases covered by the agreement.
Fees that NGCP has already paid will be recognized as satisfying its obligations in the covered cases.The past collections and future fees will be remitted to the National Treasury.

The ERC, however, did not disclose the total amount covered under the compromise agreement, how much had already been collected from NGCP, and how much is left to collect. (READ: No more VAT on system loss in electricity bills starting October)

“For years, this dispute stood in the way of a clear and settled understanding between the ERC and NGCP on the nature of these fees. This Compromise Agreement finally puts that question to rest, in a manner that respects the ERC’s mandate, gives NGCP the certainty it has sought, and ensures that the public benefits through funds that will now flow to the National Treasury,” ERC Chairperson Francis Juan said.
The agreement was signed by Juan and NGCP president and CEO Anthony Almeda during a visit by NGCP officials led by Henry T. Sy Jr., vice chairman of NGCP and son of SM founder Henry Sy Sr.

The settlement is not yet final. The ERC and NGCP said they will submit the agreement to the Supreme Court and Court of Appeals for approval within 30 days, after which they will await the courts’ action. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Former soldier exposes how Canadian white supremacist group recruits members
articles.byline: Eric Szeto, Jordan Pearson, Christian Paas-Lang, Ivan Angelovski

image.caption: Second Sons Canada requires prospective members to sign a non-disclosure agreement before they can join, according to a former soldier who attempted to join the group before learning its true nature. (Second Sons Canada/Telegram, CBC)

blocks.text: Second Sons Canada describes itself as a "men's nationalist club" dedicated to fitness and preserving Canada's heritage, but a former military member who attempted to join the group says he only learned about its true nature — which includes adoration for Hitler, neo-Nazis and hatred for Jews — when he met them in person.

Not only was the prospective member told to sign a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) that would ban him from revealing confidential information about the group, the recruit said he was also searched for recording devices and asked to say racial slurs as a test.

"They advertise themselves as one thing," said the former CAF member, who CBC News is not naming due to concerns for his personal safety and legal retribution. "And then as soon as I met them … the sheets were pulled down and it was a whole other thing that was disgusting."
He said much of the in-person meeting was about how Jewish people were evil and how Hitler's philosophy was "genius."

"They really, really wanted to know my knowledge of their version of racial ideology history and how it influences today's society," he said. "It seems like they really want to brainwash their new candidates into hatred. And that really put me off."
The former CAF member's account is the first glimpse CBC has gotten into the inner workings of the Second Sons in-person recruitment process.

Previous reporting by CBC's visual investigations team aligns with the source's information. The group itself maintains a carefully-curated image on its official social media platforms. Its leaders, meanwhile, have praised Hitler and the Nazi party, said they welcome neo-Nazis into their ranks and called for mass deportations at gunpoint and the execution of Canadian politicians while talking on personal podcasts and livestreams.

items: 'The Nazis were right': What the leaders of Canada's biggest 'nationalist' group really want

blocks.text: "The organization is clearly anxious about individuals coming forward, speaking to the press or others about their activities," said Richard Moon, Law Foundation Chair at the College of Law, University of Saskatchewan focusing on freedom of expression.

"I think there's a real risk that an NDA like this might have a chilling effect on someone's speech, and particularly on their speaking to the media or the legal authorities about activity they may be concerned about as unlawful."
Since forming in 2024, Second Sons has expanded rapidly. There are chapters across the country.

The group is part of what's known as the "active club" movement, a decentralized assortment of male-focused groups promoting white supremacist ideals. The movement has grown globally in recent years, increasingly moving from online forums to real-world training groups and anti-immigration protests.
Second Sons even folded Quebec-based Frontenac AC — one of Canada's most prominent active clubs — into their group.
Earlier this year, a government report said the active club movement posed a risk of "extreme violence."

items: 'Active clubs' are all over Canada. What are they?
'We will not be intimidated,' Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc chief says of white nationalist gathering

blocks.text: Over the weekend, Second Sons held a demonstration at Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc reserve near a former residential school, also appearing on a Kamloops overpass with a banner that read "Got bones?" The demonstration was condemned by community members and Prime Minister Mark Carney.

"The cowardly act that took place at Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc yesterday, is abhorrent. It has no place in this country. My thoughts are with everyone who are shaken and hurt by this disgusting display of hate," Carney wrote in an X post Monday.
The RCMP say they are taking the matter seriously and "will continue to engage the group as part of our response and current ongoing investigation."

On Tuesday, Second Sons president Jeremy MacKenzie reshared a doctored image to Telegram showing Second Sons members holding the "Got bones?" banner in front of the Auschwitz death camp, where the Nazis killed nearly one million Jews.
White supremacist 'media organization'
The non-disclosure agreement says Second Sons is federally registered as a numbered company: 16130623 Canada Inc.
Corporate documents found in the federal registry of businesses list Jeremy MacKenzie as director, along with Alex Vriend and Alex Cabana as shareholders.

MacKenzie is an Afghan war veteran and the founder and president of Second Sons and its predecessor, Diagolon. RCMP have described Diagolon as an "extremist, militia-like organization." Vriend is a long-time associate of MacKenzie and the vice-president of Second Sons.

Cabana has not been as openly associated with Second Sons as MacKenzie and Vriend. He is an Afghan war veteran who was affiliated with Veterans 4 Freedom, an advocacy group that was formed by central figures in the self-described "freedom convoy" protests that overtook downtown Ottawa in the winter of 2022.
It's not clear how much revenue the corporation has generated because required annual financial filings for the company in 2025 and 2026 are listed as "overdue."

The Second Sons website notes that people trying to join the group must pay an application fee, with a $20 monthly commitment if they are accepted. In livestreams on the video-sharing platform Rumble, Vriend has claimed that the group's leadership don't get paid themselves and rely on income from subscriptions by fans.
A post in the Second Sons public Telegram channel says they are working to set up a "support shop" for the group.

items: Canadian, U.S. fascist fight clubs joining forces south of the border, CBC investigation finds
A white nationalist group visiting Canadian locations is trying to normalize extremism, says a former neo-Nazi

blocks.text: But experts say there are questions about whether the company, which describes itself in the NDA as a "media organization that creates, develops and publishes content," should be allowed to operate due to the nature of its activities.

"Calling for the execution of a politician is not a legitimate activity of any company, let alone a media company," said Richard LeBlanc, professor of governance, law and ethics at York University, who reviewed the documents that CBC located.

The leaders of Second Sons appear to be aware of the rules that a registered company must follow — for example, human rights laws that ban discrimination based on race — and how the organization skirts them.

Addressing a viewer question about the group's admission process in a September 2025 livestream, Vriend said, "Second Sons is an officially-registered organization … I can't speak to what Second Sons' policy is, but in Canada, it is illegal to discriminate based on immutable characteristics like race, gender, disability, et cetera … Can I make that more clear for you? We are an organization that takes members based on meritocracy. Can you read between the lines?"

LeBlanc says if a company is engaging in overly broad NDAs, hate speech, excessive anonymity or face coverings, "that doesn't insulate the company and the founders and the officers and directors and employees of said company from liability and possibly prosecution."

The company's regulatory compliance practices may lead to its failure before anything else. The Government of Canada's website states that it has sent a notice of intent to dissolve the corporation if it does not file its financial statements "immediately."
'They were very cautious'
The former CAF member said he was looking to belong to a community that espoused patriotic views, so he decided to apply after seeing Second Sons content online.

The Second Sons website states that it welcomes former members of the armed forces, if they can show that they are no longer serving. Recently, the group's training — which initially focused on mixed martial arts sparring — has taken on a more military-style feel, including cot-carrying, army crawls and other drills.

items: Large white supremacist meeting shakes residents of Alberta town
No place for 'hate' or 'divisiveness': Politicians condemn white nationalist group's visit to northern Ontario

blocks.text: The source said he did a virtual interview over messaging app Telegram. Following that, they agreed to set up a meeting in Ontario.

"They had me pull my shirt down to make sure I wasn't wearing a wire," he said. "They had me leave my phone face up on the table to show I wasn't recording them. They were very cautious that I would leave first and not follow them."
He said they also spoke about training in hand-to-hand combat skills to prepare for potential violent situations.
Vriend, the vice-president, has publicly advocated for brutally beating counter-protesters.

Referring to a 2025 incident where a man grabbed a flag from the leader of a "Canada First" demonstration, Vriend said the response should have included the leader spearing the man in the face, cross-checking him and punching and kicking him in the head.
"Is he arrested? Yes. Does he catch a charge? Yes. Is it the end of his life? No. Does that immediately become a symbol of resistance for all Canadians? Yes."
CBC's source said he did not learn the names of the men he met.
Undercover applicant

The application process mirrors what happened when two La Presse journalists, Tristan Peloquin and Vincent Poirier, applied to join Second Sons over the summer, under a false name. The existence of the NDA was first reported by La Presse. CBC obtained it independently.

Shortly after applying, the two La Presse journalists received an email that included 17 questions asking for their name, family history in Canada and political beliefs. From there, they were messaged on Telegram by someone from Second Sons — who turned out to be the former leader of Frontenac Active Club, Shawn Beauvais-MacDonald, who has referred to himself online as a Nazi and praised Hitler.
"He was trying to have more information on why we wanted to join Second Sons. And after that, in the first 24 hours, he asked us for a meetup. We were surprised," Poirier told CBC News.

Second Sons also sent a non-disclosure agreement to the journalists, saying that the document "not only legally protects our Organization and its members, it also protects you from having any of the personal information you provide released under penalty of law."
La Presse did not meet in person with Second Sons.
Second Sons did not respond to CBC's request for comment.
Do you have more information on this story? Email us at vi@cbc.ca

articles.title: Families of Canadian mining firm workers kidnapped in Mexico plan to file RCMP complaint

image.caption: A view inside the gated residential compound of Vizsla Silver Corp., in Concordia, Mexico, about 35 kilometres east of Mazatlán. The site, now sealed by Sinaloa state's Attorney General's Office, is believed to be the place where 10 Vizsla Silver workers were kidnapped on Jan. 23, 2026. Nine of thei

blocks.text: The families of the workers of a Canadian mining firm kidnapped earlier this year by a suspected cartel commando squad in the violence-torn Mexican state of Sinaloa plan to file an RCMP complaint against the Vancouver-based company, their lawyer says.

Canada's federal police force needs to probe whether Vizsla Silver Corp.'s on-site management had allegedly established some level of co-ordination with an organized armed group in a region, said Odracir Ricardo Espinoza, who represents the families of seven kidnapped workers.

Vizsla Silver's exploration area is dominated by warring factions of the Sinaloa cartel, which is a designated terror organization in Canada. Mexican authorities have said the workers were kidnapped by one of the cartel's factions.
"Imagine a puzzle, and you're getting piece, after piece, after piece," said Espinoza. "But we don't have the most complicated, darkest pieces. The company has those pieces."

Early in the morning of Jan. 23, armed men stormed a gated compound in Concordia, Sinaloa, where Vizsla Silver housed its workers and parked some of its vehicles, kidnapping 10 of the company's workers.

Two weeks later, Mexican authorities located the bodies of nine of the workers in clandestine graves dug into an open field in El Verde, a village about 19 kilometres northwest of Concordia. The whereabouts of the 10th worker, Francisco Antonio Esparza Yáñez, who was responsible for community relations, remain unknown.
The motive behind the kidnapping remains unclear.
Calls for probe of alleged dealings

According to family testimony, all Vizsla Silver workers were instructed to wear a specific colour of vest so they would be identified as part of the company by the organized crime group that controlled the area, said Espinoza.

"Someone had to tell them, 'Put that on so we don't do anything to you,'" said Espinoza. "And that wasn't an intermediary. That had to be one of their [organized crime group] members. So those conversations, those acts should have been denounced."

Two former Vizsla Silver workers also previously told CBC News that on-site company management told them to switch from orange to yellow vests and helmets, so the armed men who patrolled the territory would know they were with the company.
"One of the fronts we plan to open is a complaint with the Mounted Police in Canada," said Espinoza, adding they also plan to take the issue to U.S. authorities.
Vizsla Silver Corp. trades on the New York and Toronto stock exchanges.

items: Local management had dealings with armed group before kidnapping at Canadian mining company, say ex-workers
Mexico living through 'terror,' says relative of kidnapped employee of Canadian mining company

blocks.text: The families say the Attorney General's Office of Mexico has not yet compelled Vizsla Silver to turn over evidence they believe the company holds related to the Jan. 23 kidnapping, and if that does not happen, they plan to seek a judicial order in Mexican court.
They want Mexican authorities to request that top company officials, including the CEO, provide testimony, Espinoza said.

In an emailed statement, Vizsla Silver said it was limited in its ability to comment because the matter was under an "active investigation," but the company "continues to co-operate fully" with Mexican authorities and has provided all requested information.

"We fully understand and share the families' desire for answers, and we appreciate how extraordinarily difficult the continued uncertainty is, particularly for the family of our colleague who remains missing," said the statement.
Military to set up on site

In a podcast earlier this month, Vizsla Silver CEO Michael Konnert said the company had "endeavoured to support the families substantially," and it had plans for a foundation "to support the families of our lost colleagues and coworkers."
Konnert said a military installation would soon be placed on the project site, with "other kinds of supporting infrastructure for the security apparatus."
The federal Attorney General's Office did not return a request for comment.

Vizsla Silver's exploration operations are spread across territory that has reportedly seen some of the fiercest fighting between factions of the Sinaloa cartel in a two-year-long civil war within what was once one of the world's biggest drug smuggling organizations.

The war has led to thousands of deaths and disappearances across the state and the displacement of hundreds of families from the Concordia area, according to a July report from the International Crisis Group, a global non-profit NGO.

The Canadian mining firm — which never filed a formal complaint following the kidnapping — is conducting exploration work across 35,000 hectares rich with silver in a remote, mountainous region as part of its flagship Panuco Project, which sits roughly 25 kilometres east of Concordia's urban centre.

items: Canadian mining company employees worked amid gunfire, Mexican cartel checkpoints, says family member

blocks.text: Company should turn over evidence

The families believe Vizsla Silver holds vital information it has yet to turn over to Mexican authorities that could shed light on the motive behind the Jan. 23 kidnapping and subsequent killings, Espinoza said.

Specifically, he said, the company needs to hand over security camera footage from its complex, GPS information from its vehicles, corporate cellphones and records, and internal company communication related to the kidnapping.
The families are also seeking testimony from one of the company's legal representatives who alerted authorities about the kidnapping, Espinoza said.
"The company has not participated in the investigation, it hasn't presented information that it should have presented," he said.

items: Family wants killing of young engineer linked with case of kidnapped Canadian mining firm workers
Probe alleging 'El Chapo' sons fed victims to tigers led to case against top Mexican politician: court docs

blocks.text: At one point, in the window between the kidnapping and discovery of bodies, that representative told families that a hospital in Mazatlan was preparing to receive the kidnapped worker.
"We need to know her testimony," said Espinoza. "Where did this [information] about the hospital come from? Was it just to calm the families? Or did she have some other type of information?"

The families are also seeking information around Vizsla Silver's security protocols and its decision to keep working in a volatile area. The company had paused work in April 2025 over security concerns.
Some family members have recordings that capture the sounds of gunbattles, sent to them by their loved ones while working for Vizsla Silver, Espinoza said.
"They kept working because they had to provide for their children," he said.
Alan Esparza, the son of the missing worker Antonio Esparza Yáñez, said the company has done little to help in the search for his father.
"It's like the earth swallowed him. It's incredible, really, that I know absolutely nothing," he said in an interview with CBC News.
Esparza said he last saw his father on Jan. 3, after the family spent New Year's together. His father was planning to soon retire, he said.
"What has Vizsla done for its employees to prevent what happened, to fix what happened? And now, what is it doing to help find the 10th?" said Esparza.
In June, a local La Chapiza-aligned cartel boss named Gabriel Nicolás Martínez Larios, also known as El Gabito or El 80, was arrested in connection with the Vizsla Silver kidnapping.
And earlier this month, Mexican authorities further announced the arrests of Angel Gabriel and Milton Yair, along with 11 others, who were part of the La Chapiza cell linked to the case.
