articles.title: Netanyahu says too early to tell who was behind plane incident as flydubai halts all flights to Israel
articles.summary:
Israeli prime minister cautions against early conclusions when asked if there were any signs of Iranian involvement

Benjamin Netanyahu has said it was too early to tell who was ultimately…

blocks.text: Benjamin Netanyahu has said it was too early to tell who was ultimately behind the apparent attempt to crash a ⁠Tel Aviv-bound flydubai flight, even as Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations called the incident a “terror attack”, without apportioning blame.

Danny Danon told Fox News on Wednesday night that Israel had “no doubt that it was a terror attack from a radical individual. We still cannot link it to a terror state or terror organisation, but for sure we know there was an intention to bring that plane down.”
Flydubai said its flights to and from Israel would be suspended while the investigation takes place and urged all parties “to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts”.

The incident – which began when one pilot stabbed another on the flight deck in an apparent attempt to take control of the aircraft – is under investigation. The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had more than 170 people on board, most of them from Israel.

In what have been hailed as acts of tremendous bravery, several passenger rushed the cockpit of the flight and wrestled the controls from the alleged attacker even as the plane descended sharply, managing to eventually taking control and stabilising the plane before making an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, told Fox News host Sean Hannity: “We’ll get to the root of ⁠this attacker, whether he had accomplices” but cautioned that it was “too early to say” when asked whether there was any indication of Iranian involvement.

The pilot accused of carrying out the stabbing was being questioned by Saudi authorities, the Israeli prime minister said, adding that he expected he would soon be taken to the UAE, where the flight took off from. Netanyahu said earlier that he had spoken with the UAE’s president, who agreed that Israel would join the interrogation of the suspect.
Israeli officials, speaking on condition of anonymity to reporters, said the attacker was an Omani national, but there was no comment from Oman or the UAE.

Israel’s foreign ministry later briefed its diplomats around the world that the incident was an “attempted terrorist attack against Israelis, the United Arab Emirates, and the Abraham Accords,” referring to the deal that normalised relations between the two countries in 2020.

But on Wednesday evening Donald Trump told reporters the incident remained unclear, after he had spoken to Netanyahu. “It seems as though the co-pilot was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack-job, and he stabbed the pilot,” the US president told reporters in the Oval Office.
Netanyahu was among the world leaders celebrating the bravery of the passengers and crew of the flydubai flight on Wednesday.
A video shared by the prime minister’s office showed passenger Yaniv Hayoun, a plumber, speaking to Netanyahu at length about how the events on board played out.

Hayoun told the prime minister how he and other passengers heard screaming and felt the air pressure change as the plane dived before they forced their way into the cockpit and found the attacker at the instrument panel.
“I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and dragged him out first,” Hayoun said during the meeting with Netanyahu after the plane had landed safely and the passengers were flown to Israel.
As others wrestled with the attacker, Hayoun said he grabbed the controls and pulled them the way he had seen on television. Then other crew members took over.

The stabbed pilot was identified as Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar, who was said to have made the emergency call and opened the door to the cockpit, allowing others to rush in and subdue the attacker.

In a post on X early on Thursday, Indian prime minister Narendra Modi lauded Machchhar a “hero”. “In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously ‌injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others. His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy,” Modi ​said.
Machchhar, an Indian citizen from Mumbai, is being treated in a hospital in Saudi Arabia’s north-western city of Tabuk, where the plane landed safely.

articles.title: Israelis divided as vote that could oust Netanyahu only weeks away
articles.summary:
Some on streets of Jerusalem pledge their support to prime minister while others hope for change

On the streets of Jerusalem, crowded with secular and ultra-Orthodox Jews, religious…
articles.byline: Lorenzo Tondo and Quique Kierszenbaum in Jerusalem; graphics by Ana Lucía González Paz

blocks.text: On the streets of Jerusalem, crowded with secular and ultra-Orthodox Jews, religious nationalists, settlers, Palestinians, and soldiers returning from deployments, uncertainty hangs over an election less than a month away that could mark a turning point for a country profoundly changed after the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023 and nearly three years of war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
The political battle remains on a knife-edge.
For over two years most polls have predicted that the coalition of parties led by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu will collectively slip below the 61-seat threshold needed to form a government.

But there is no clear path to power for his main opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, the former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, even if he maintains current levels of support, because he has ruled out going into coalition with any of the parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel, who are projected to claim a critical 12 seats.

For Netanyahu to stay in power, he would have to either put together a different coalition or pull off an unprecedented election night surprise. Another deeply fragmented Knesset seems likely, in which neither side is close to securing a majority.

The latest Channel 13 poll, published last week, captured that deadlock: Jewish Israeli parties opposed to Netanyahu were projected to win 52 seats, against 51 for the prime minister’s bloc, with both falling short of the 61 required for a majority.

Eisenkot’s Yashar party topped the poll with 22 seats, while Netanyahu’s Likud was projected to take 18. The lack of clarity over the next government – with both main blocs on the right – is fuelling unease among Israelis, some of whom believe little will change whoever becomes prime minister.

“I’m not going to vote because I don’t trust anyone,” said Rachel, 42, an Israeli citizen living in West Jerusalem. “I used to vote for Yair Lapid,” she added, referring to the leader of the centrist Yesh Atid party. “The party’s name means ‘there is a future’. But today, I don’t see any future for this country.”
Average public trust across the eight Israeli institutions measured consistently by the Israel Democracy Institute, a statistics body, stood at 34% in 2025, compared with 61% in 2012.

An atmosphere of pessimism and indecision is palpable in Jerusalem, where tensions between Palestinians in occupied East Jerusalem – the majority of whom cannot vote in Israeli national elections – and rightwing Jewish Israelis have deepened since 7 October. The Hamas attack is likely to weigh heavily on the ballot: a recent poll by the Israel Democracy Institute found that 68% of Jewish respondents said 7 October would be a central factor in deciding how they voted.

“After 7 October, everyone in this government has to take the blame,” said Ilda, who owns a clothing shop on Jaffa Street, one of Jerusalem’s oldest and busiest thoroughfares. Referring to a Haaretz investigation claiming Netanyahu had been warned about the possibility of a major Hamas attack, which he denies, she said: “After journalists exposed what happened, look what they did: they attacked the journalists instead of taking responsibility.”

West Jerusalem has long been considered fertile ground for Netanyahu and the Israeli right. Yet Israel’s growing diplomatic isolation and the prospect of seemingly endless conflict on multiple fronts are beginning to worry voters even here, a few steps from the bustling Mahane Yehuda market, where giant election posters for Itamar Ben-Gvir, the far-right national security minister known for his anti-Palestinian rhetoric and championing a racist death penalty law that in practice applies only to Palestinians, loom over the streets.

blocks.caption: Another advert showing Ben-Gvir at the Machane Yehuda market in Jerusalem.  Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: “This country needs radical change. I think I’ll vote for Naftali Bennett,” said Yosef, 26, a religious Israeli, referring to the rightwing former prime minister who now leads the B’Yachad alliance and is one of Netanyahu’s main political rivals.

On one side are tens of thousands of Netanyahu supporters – called “Bibi-ists” in reference to the prime minister’s nickname – as well as backers of the far-right ministers Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, who want to return the current coalition to power to “finish the job” in Gaza, Iran, Lebanon and the West Bank.

On the other are tens of thousands of voters who believe Israel is losing its standing in the world and needs a change of direction – something many see as embodied by the centre-right Eisenkot. His supporters argue that he would place greater emphasis on education, social policy and the economy, areas they say have been neglected by the current government.

“I’ll vote for anyone but the prime minister of 7 October,” said Turgeman as he enjoyed a coffee with his wife at a cafe in Jaffa during the Jewish high holiday season. “I’ve never voted Likud in my life, and I’m certainly not going to start now. I’ll vote for Eisenkot. We need a normal prime minister – someone who also cares about the economy and about prices, which have soared because of the war.”

Food prices in Israel have reached record highs amid the regional conflict and supply chain disruption, with food inflation outpacing the broader consumer price index. The cost of food, including fresh fruit and vegetables, has risen by 9.5% over the past two years.

“They think about wars, while nobody is dealing with the economic crisis,” Turgeman said. “And what has Netanyahu done? He has continued to provide financial support that benefits the Haredi [ultra-Orthodox] community.”

Since 7 October, Israel’s ultra-Orthodox community has been at the centre of a bitter dispute over military conscription. While most Jewish Israelis serve, Haredi men studying in religious seminaries have long been largely exempt.

In 2024, amid war and growing pressure on reservists, the supreme court ruled there was no legal basis to continue the exemption, fuelling anti-draft protests, roadblocks and clashes with police. Haredi parties have blamed Netanyahu for failing to pass legislation to protect the exemption.

Ultra-Orthodox Jews, who make up about 14% of Israel’s population, have traditionally voted for parties backed by their rabbis, including the two main Haredi parties in Netanyahu’s coalition. But anger among younger Haredim over conscription and the policing of protests could lead some to defy their religious leaders this time.

“All the options in this election are junk, but I think I will vote for Eisenkot,” said Pinchas, 24, an ultra-Orthodox student who recently completed his military service. “I have the impression that this time people my age won’t vote according to what the rabbis tell them. Many are angry about the way Netanyahu handled the conscription law, and especially about the crackdown on those who protested against it.”

As the Guardian conducted interviews near Jerusalem’s central bus station, an elderly passerby called out: “There is only one prime minister – Bibi!” It was a reminder that, despite the uncertainty and the opposition’s narrow lead in the polls, the Israeli leader retains a loyal base.

blocks.caption: An advert for Gadi Eisenkot, a retired chief of staff of the Israeli army, on a bus in Jerusalem. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: “I’m sure Netanyahu will win,” said Avraham Levy, 76, a Likud supporter and fruit seller at Mahane Yehuda market. “We’ll have the majority. We need to support Netanyahu because he has to finish the job. If he doesn’t, who will?” he said, referring to Israel’s wars on several fronts.

Among those still backing Netanyahu’s coalition partners are supporters of the far right, including Jakub, 23, who was due to begin his military service soon. “I’ll vote for Moshe Feiglin,” he said, referring to an extreme far-right former Israeli Knesset member who declared in 2025 that the conflict in Gaza was not against Hamas but against every child and baby in the territory, and is now running jointly with the far-right Religious Zionist party. “Because he represents my values, and he has never changed his principles,” Jakub said.

The field is wide open and the divide is also generational: by 2019, support for a Palestinian state stood at about 20%-30% among the youngest Jewish Israeli cohorts, compared with roughly 40%-55% among older generations, reflecting a longer-term shift towards more hawkish attitudes. No more recent comparable data was available.
The difficulty for the anti-Netanyahu camp is that it remains fragmented and has struggled to agree on a coherent political platform or a common strategy capable of uniting its different factions.

Parties representing Palestinian citizens, known as Arab parties inside Israel, could push Eisenkot’s coalition over the 61-seat threshold, but amid a campaign of racism and Islamophobia, he has ruled out going into government with them.
They could potentially support a minority government.

But last week, the Central Elections Committee voted to bar Ra’am and the Joint List, the country’s two main Palestinian parties, from the election, after the far-right Otzma Yehudit party filed a petition arguing that they support terrorism and deny the existence of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state.

The opposition Democrats party filed a similar petition arguing for Otzma Yehudit to be banned for incitement to racism and negating the existence of Israel as a democratic state, because of racist policies pursued in power under its leader Itamar Ben Gvir. That was not upheld.
The decision is being challenged in the supreme court, which has overturned similar bans in past elections.
If allowed to run in the elections, the Arab parties will be crucial to the opposition’s prospects of forming a government and to Eisenkot’s chances of replacing Netanyahu.

Tensions between Palestinian citizens of Israel and the state have deepened since 7 October amid arrests, interrogations and other legal action against Arab citizens, often over protests or social media posts.

blocks.caption: Avraham Levy at his fruit stall in the Mahane Yehuda market. Behind him is an image of Menachem Begin, a co-founder of the Likud party. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: For these reasons, Palestinian citizens of Israel are often reluctant to express their voting preferences. In the 2025 Israeli Democracy Index survey, 70% said they preferred to remain silent about their political views in the presence of strangers, up from 45% in 2016 and compared with 53% of Jewish respondents.

But Palestinian citizens of Israel remain divided over how best to respond, with many pessimistic that any future government will defend rights they say have too often been denied. The Joint List has maintained a more oppositional stance, signalling it could support an anti-Netanyahu minority government from outside while stopping short of joining a coalition, although it has done so in the past.

“These elections are about our strength as an Arab community and our ability to have an influential political voice,” said Amir, 34, from Mashhad in northern Israel, who plans to vote for the Joint List. “We need strong, united Arab representation on equality, discrimination and the Palestinian cause, while cooperating when it benefits our community.”

Ra’am, led by Mansour Abbas, has instead made political pragmatism its defining strategy. In 2021 it became the first independent Arab party to join an Israeli governing coalition, seeking budgets, services and greater influence for Palestinian citizens of Israel.

“Arab society is being torn apart by crime and violence, while relations with Jewish Israelis are becoming more hostile,” said Abu Mahmoud, 33, from Kafr Kanna, also in the north of the country. “That’s why I’ll vote for Ra’am: negotiate, secure budgets and work with Jewish Israelis where possible.”
He added: “I want politics that can actually improve people’s lives.”
Jamal Risheq contributed to this report

articles.title: New Google Maps images reveal massive scale of devastation in Gaza
articles.summary:
Satellite imagery shows further destruction of homes, businesses and places of worship since fragile ceasefire

An update to Google Maps has revealed the extent of devastation during the…

blocks.text: An update to Google Maps has revealed the extent of devastation during the three-year Gaza war and the severity of the continuing humanitarian crisis faced by the territory’s 2.3 million inhabitants.
The images were taken in June this year and show further destruction of homes, businesses, places of worship and infrastructure since a fragile ceasefire came into effect almost 12 months ago.

blocks.caption: Gaza 2023-2026: al-Mawasi, Rafah

blocks.text: They show huge tented camps lining much of the shoreline, often within a few metres of the sea. Gaza’s once busy main port, now badly damaged and empty of fishing boats, is surrounded by makeshift accommodation. Any available open space in Gaza City is packed with shacks, tents and huts.

blocks.caption: Gaza 2023-2026: Tel al-Sultan, Rafah

blocks.text: The images also show massive damage to northern towns such as Beit Lahiya and Beit Hanoun, as well as the destruction of places of worship such as the Istiqlal mosque in Khan Younis. Major neighbourhoods in Gaza City such as Jabaliya and Shuja’iya, which were targeted in repeated Israeli offensives, are clearly now uninhabitable.

Swaths of rubble are visible in the south of Gaza, where a wide strip appears to have been cleared by Israeli forces along the border with Egypt. The town of Rafah appears to have been almost entirely reduced to rubble and Tel al-Sultan razed to the ground.

blocks.caption: Gaza 2023-2026: Istiqlal Mosque, Khan Younis

blocks.text: More than 2.1 million displaced people are living in tents and temporary shelters in Gaza, where about 82% of structures – roughly 200,000 buildings – have been damaged, with about two-thirds of those destroyed, according to the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, Unrwa.
A recent UN assessment estimated that the number of destroyed structures across Gaza had increased by 9% since the declaration of a ceasefire in October 2025.

blocks.caption: Gaza 2023-2026: Beit Lahiya

blocks.text: “The estimate of the total amount of rubble in Gaza is 61m tonnes. It is approximately 20 times the amount of rubble generated in all wars across the world over the last 18 years,” Jaco Cilliers, the UN Development Programme’s special representative in Palestine told the Guardian last month. The presence of human remains still buried under the rubble remains one of the most urgent humanitarian problems.

More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the start of the war, mostly civilians. The conflict was triggered by a surprise attack by Hamas into Israel in October 2023, in which militants killed about 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and took 251 others hostage.

articles.title: ‘Explosion of melt rates’: 20% of Swiss glaciers lost in five years
articles.summary:
Alpine regions in Europe experiencing extreme glacier collapse due to heat-trapping effects of fossil fuel pollution

Switzerland has lost almost one-fifth of its ice in just five years,…

blocks.text: Switzerland has lost almost one-fifth of its ice in just five years, research has found, in a dramatic reshaping of the Alpine country whose big white glaciers have been reduced to moonlike rock deserts, scientists say.

Swiss glaciers shrank by 5.5% in the first eight months of 2026, according to an annual monitoring report, after a summer of scorching heatwaves that followed a winter with little snow. The reduction in ice volume falls just shy of the record set in 2022 and brings the total loss of glacier ice since 2021 to 19.4%.

blocks.caption: Glaciologist Matthias Huss records changes in the Scex Rouge glacier above Les Diablerets, western Switzerland. Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: Matthias Huss, a glaciologist at ETH Zürich and lead author of the report, said many people do not realise how fast glaciers are retreating, or that just one generation ago some now-barren sites used to sit beneath hundreds of metres of ice. The scientists have not yet compiled a formal tally of lost glaciers this year but said they had witnessed the death of a number of small ones.

“I visited one last week and it’s so impressive to stand in this moonlike landscape where there was a big layer of ice – an extensive glacier – just a few years ago,” said Huss. “And now it’s a rock desert where there’s some scattered blocks of old ice still lying around and melting on the hot rocks.”

The report, a collaboration between the Swiss Glacier Monitoring Network and the Swiss Commission for Cryosphere Observation, found the mean thickness of individual glaciers fell by between 2.5 metres and 4 metres in 2026. Huss said scientists were increasingly seeing glaciers collapse from the inside – the result of internal streams beneath the ice that excavate caverns – rather than simply retreating from surface heat.

blocks.caption: Matthias Huss looks at the ice on the Rhône glacier in Obergoms, Switzerland. Photograph: Pierre Albouy/Reuters

blocks.text: “You have huge holes like cheese in the middle of the ice that have collapsing roofs,” said Huss. “These are processes that tear the glaciers apart and make them retreat even faster.”

Europe is warming twice as fast as the global average from the heat-trapping effects of fossil fuel pollution and the destruction of nature, with Alpine regions experiencing some of the most dramatic changes.

Analysis published by MeteoSwiss on Tuesday found the summer half-year from April to September was the hottest and driest it had been since records began in 1864. In that time, humanity has filled the atmosphere with 1.8tn tons of carbon dioxide and heated the planet by about 1.4C.

The heat this summer was worse than in 2022 but Swiss ice loss just missed the record-breaking levels set that year. The scientists attributed this to limited deposits of Saharan dust, which foul the snow and prevent it from reflecting sunlight, as well as slightly greater snow cover at the end of winter and more sunlight in the summer.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Two mountaineers hiking on the Rhône Glacier, above Gletsch, in the Swiss Alps. Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: Huss visited the former Plattalvafirn, or Griess glacier, in September, which used to cover a mountain flank but lost 99% of its area in just 20 years. The glacier was the subject of some of the most detailed monitoring in the world in the 1950s and Huss worked with its data when he was a PhD student.

“What was different at that time, is that the rates of retreat were still kind of at a normal level,” said Huss. “What we are seeing now is a complete explosion of these melt rates, leading to the disintegration of glaciers. They’re really just falling apart.”

articles.title: Kyiv Independent editor: ‘Our readers want Russia to suffer but we can’t be propagandists’
articles.summary:
Olga Rudenko says news site has duty to report on Russian military gains and Ukrainian corruption even if subjects are not so well read

Readers of Ukraine’s leading English news site “really…

blocks.text: Readers of Ukraine’s leading English news site “really want Russia to suffer” but that should not lead the title to downplay the military and political problems facing Kyiv, its editor has said.

Speaking to the Guardian before an event to London, Olga Rudenko said many of the Kyiv Independent’s most-read stories described Ukrainian deep strike attacks into Russia, potentially distorting its coverage.

The Kyiv Independent, however, cannot afford to become propagandistic, she argued, and marginalise Russian military successes or reduce reporting on Ukrainian corruption because the subjects are not so well read.
“We had a conversation in the newsroom when somebody raised that our website, in the mornings, is all about Ukrainian attacks on Russian Wildberries warehouses and so on,” Rudenko said.
“But it’s misrepresenting the full picture when you don’t balance it out with enough stories about attacks on Ukraine, which are, by the way, far less popular with our readers.”
The challenge is that “people really want Russia to suffer”, and read about “something going boom” but it was the Kyiv Independent’s duty to “not just to feed them more of what they like”.

blocks.caption: Olga Rudenko: ‘It’s misrepresenting the full picture when you don’t balance it out with enough stories about attacks on Ukraine.’ Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian

blocks.text: The “core idea of the Kyiv Independent is that we’re not Ukrainian propaganda, we’re not affiliated with the government, we’re not doing we’re not Ukraine’s PR service,” the editor said.

Rudenko said she had “no expectation” that the war would end any time soon, with Russia stepping up its bombing of Kyiv before winter and Ukrainian strikes denting its neighbour’s economy while diplomacy is stalled.

It is a feeling that has hung over journalists at the site for some time. This year employees did not bother planning for a peacetime scenario in their annual strategy session. “It was the first time when this question wasn’t really arising,” Rudenko said.

On Friday, Rudenko will host a “live story-telling event” in London where reporters, including the frontline correspondent Francis Farrell, will give their personal experience of Ukraine in the midst of the biggest war in Europe since 1945.

The title relies on readers to make monthly contributions for its revenue, an idea also used by the Guardian, and London was chosen as a venue because it “is probably the biggest city in terms of membership”, the editor said.

Media freedom in Ukraine has not worsened under Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Rudenko said, but added: “I would struggle to say it has gotten better.” Reporters can write freely without “fearing some immediate consequences” but the editor said that a concentration of power around the president remains.

Zelenskyy has not held a press conference for independent Ukrainian media since February 2025, and there is still a bitter legacy from the president’s attempt a few months later to neutralise Ukraine’s two anti-corruption agencies, which had to be reversed in the light of public protests.
after newsletter promotion

“We’ve been casting a critical look at Zelenskyy and his government for a while now, she said, highlighting an editorial written last July at the height of crisis, headlined “Zelenskyy just betrayed Ukraine’s democracy”.

The president and his allies, Rudenko said, had “brazenly and stupidly” sought to take away a central achievement of the Ukrainian revolution of 2014, after which the independence of Ukraine’s anti-corruption bodies was introduced.

Despite this, she said, “a critical mass of Ukrainians” do not think it is time to hold a presidential election, as called for by the former defence minister Mykhalio Fedorov in August. Elections have been suspended under martial law, though Zelenskyy’s term expired more than two years ago.

The Kyiv Independent has not come out in support of elections, Rudenko said, partly because support for holding them is running at about 15%. Protests this summer against Fedorov’s firing by Zelenskyy were “of the size that the president can still afford to ignore”, she added.
The Kyiv Independent was founded three months before the full-scale Russian invasion by journalists who had lost their jobs when the rival Kyiv Post was temporarily closed by its owner.
Launched with a $100,000 grant, it rapidly became an essential English language news sources for Ukraine as the country was attacked and the war with Russia became global news.

The number of contributing readers, or members, most of whom pay $5 a month, has risen from 14,000 at the beginning of 2025 to 25,500 a year later and to 36,000 now, allowing staff numbers to grow to 99 and the title to move to bigger offices.

articles.title: Swiss glaciers lose more than 5% in ice volume in 2026
articles.summary: Over the last five years, Swiss glaciers have lost nearly 20% of their mass, and 2026 saw the second-biggest loss of glacier volume on record. Experts warn there could be no ice left in the next…

image.caption: Scientists have warned of the total loss of the Swiss glaciers in the coming yearsImage: FABRICE COFFRINI/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Glaciers in Switzerland have lost nearly 20% of their mass in five years, experts said Thursday.
The experts said Swiss glaciers are melting rapidly and this year saw the second-biggest drop on record due to unprecedented heat waves in Europe.
There was a drop of 5.5% of Swiss glaciers this year, the Glacier Monitoring in Switzerland (GLAMOS) network found in a new study.
GLAMOS warns of total glacier loss
According to the report, over the past five years, the Swiss glaciers have lost almost ​a fifth of their ice, warning that in the future it could threaten water supplies.
The report also raised questions about the long-term survival of Europe's ice fields.
"Alpine glaciers have no chance of surviving in the long term under such conditions," said GLAMOS chief Matthias Huss. "The glaciers this year have lost enormous quantities of ice."
Little winter snowfall and record summer temperatures led Huss to call 2026 "a catastrophic year."
Locals face uncertainty after Swiss Alps glacier collapse
"This is a glacier that isn't surviving," he said. "There will probably be no ice in 10 or maybe 15 years."
The GLAMOS report reiterates concerns about the impact of global warming, especially in Europe, the world's fastest-warming continent.

"The warming that we are experiencing now can be attributed 100% to anthropogenic climate change. It's as simple as that," Huss said, using the term for climate change caused by human activity. "Without human emissions or fossil fuels we wouldn't have any warming at the moment."

blocks.text: Japan has raised fees for foreigners seeking permanent residency in the country by 20 times to 200,000 yen ($1,270; £955).
Those seeking permanent residency must now also meet new income, pension and Japanese-language requirements.
Long lines formed outside immigration offices earlier this week as applicants sought to beat the fee hikes, with Tokyo's main immigration bureau reporting wait times of over seven hours.
The fee increases are part of a series of changes to Japan's immigration policy under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, which aim to manage its rapidly growing foreign population.

In July, Japan implemented a five-fold increase in visa fees for all foreigners – its first visa fee hike in 50 years. Authorities said this was meant to "reflect inflation and exchange rate fluctuations".
Although immigration remains politically sensitive and restrictive in Japan, the nation's ageing population is increasingly relying on foreign workers to plug a labour shortage.

Japan's foreign resident population surpassed 4.12 million at the end of 2025, marking a record 9.5% increase from the previous year. This however has led to growing anxieties over immigration and social change.
Takaichi has made managing immigration one of her key priorities since she took office in October last year.

In an X post days before the residency permit hikes set in, Takaichi wrote that her government recognises that "some members of the public may feel a sense of concern or unfairness" as Japan's foreign resident population grows.

"To address these concerns, [the government] is working to ensure that its policies toward foreign nationals are orderly, and that both Japanese citizens and foreign residents can live safely and securely," she wrote.
Before the hikes, it would cost non-permanent residents in Japan 6,000 yen each time they applied to change their residency status or extend their period of stay.
From 1 October, the fee varies according to the duration of stay sought – from 10,000 yen for three months or less, to 75,000 yen for five years or more.
Applicants who face financial hardship or are designated as refugees would be granted discounts.
Aspiring permanent residents must now also earn a stable income at or above the Japanese average. Latest data released in July puts average household income at 5.75 million yen as of 2024.
Micaiah Stevens, who has been living and working in Tokyo for 10 years, was not able to compile the necessary documentation to submit his application for permanent residency before the price hike.
The 37-year-old still plans to apply, but questions the new measures aimed at foreign residents.

"My immediate reaction was that foreigners were being treated a bit too conveniently. We're being asked to make more than the average Japanese person, pay a significantly higher fee, just to be able to work in Japan and provide taxes," he tells the BBC.
"There's already a significant language and cultural barrier that prevents some talent from coming over. This just doesn't strike me as a plan that was thought out to the long term."

From April next year, permanent residency applicants will face even tighter requirements, including basic Japanese language proficiency. This has led to a surge in enrollments at Japanese language schools as well as people signing up to take the Japanese-Language Proficiency Test, local media reported.

Applicants' expected pension benefits must also be equivalent to that of someone who has enrolled into the employee pension system for 30 years, although the value of one's financial assets can be considered if their expected pension benefits fall short.

articles.title: 'Hero' pilot stabbed by other pilot on Israel-bound plane, Israeli PM says
articles.summary: Passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and safely landed the plane in Saudi Arabia.

blocks.text: A pilot has been arrested after he stabbed the other pilot on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv and "apparently tried to crash the plane", Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said.
Passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and retook control of the Flydubai aircraft, landing it safely at an airport in Tabuk, northwestern Saudi Arabia, with more than 170 people on board.
The passengers, who were almost all Israeli, arrived later on Wednesday in Tel Aviv on a repatriation flight.

The stabbed pilot, named as Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar, has been taken to hospital but is reported to be in a stable condition. Netanyahu praised him as a "true hero" of "extraordinary bravery".

"Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster," Netanyahu wrote on X.
"He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals."
The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said Machchhar was in a stable condition in hospital.
Image source, EPA
Passengers arrived in Tel Aviv after their original flight was forced to land in Saudi Arabia

No motive for the incident has been given and the pilot was under investigation in Saudi Arabia, Netanyahu told Fox News on Wednesday night, before he was expected to be taken back to the United Arab Emirates (UAE), where the flight took off from.
Israel was "likely" to contribute to the investigation, the prime minister added.
US President Donald Trump said he had spoken with Netanyahu following the incident, saying it seemed as though the attacker was "perhaps a terrorist" or there were other reasons behind the attack.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has also called it an "attempted jihadist terror attack", without giving any details.
Flydubai's flight FZ1073 took off from Dubai International Airport in the UAE at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time), en route to Ben-Gurion Airport in Israel.

Around two and a half hours into its journey, data from flight tracking website Flightrader24 reported a rapid descent over Saudi Arabia, dropping more than 17,000 feet (over 5,000m) in less than two minutes.
Minutes later, the plane signalled an emergency code - squawk 7700 - before switching it to a squawk 7500 code reporting a hijacking.
Around 20 minutes after these codes were signalled, the plane looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent for landing.
Less than an hour later, the plane returned to squawk 7700.
Shortly after the incident, the Israeli and Saudi Arabian air forces dispatched fighter jets, while Netanyahu held urgent consultations.

blocks.caption: Map showing the route of Flydubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv. The plane departed Dubai at 03:05 GMT and flew northwest across Saudi Arabia towards Israel. Near the Israel-Jordan border, the aircraft declared a general emergency at 05:31 and a hijacking alert at 05:38 before turning away…

blocks.text: Initial media reports suggested a fight had broken out between the aircraft's two pilots, causing the rapid descent and landing.

However, in the hours after the plane touched down in Tabuk, eyewitness accounts and a statement by Netanyahu confirmed one of the pilots had stabbed the other and, according to the Israeli prime minister, "apparently tried to crash" the aircraft.

He said an Israeli passenger told him "the plane went into a spin and began to descend" before the passenger and a crew member entered the cockpit and overpowered the "pilot who had carried out the stabbing".
Two on-duty crew travelling on the flight were then able to land the plane safely, Flydubai said.

In an address on Wednesday evening, Netanyahu called the situation "a very serious security incident" and said Israeli security forces were "maintaining close contact with the relevant authorities to ensure the continued safety of the passengers".
Unlike Israel's defence minister, Netanyahu did not give a motive for the incident.
"I salute these heroes who demonstrated extraordinary resourcefulness and courage," he added. "They saved many lives and prevented a major disaster."

blocks.caption: A woman smiles and embraces a person draped in an Israeli flag as passengers who were on the FlyDubai aircraft bound for Israel from the United Arab Emirates are greeted by their friends and family, as they arrive at the Ben Gurion International Airport.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters

Flydubai said in a statement that "an altercation occurred in the flight deck" and the flight was "successfully secured by on-duty Flydubai crew travelling on the flight, who diverted and landed the aircraft safely at Tabuk airport".

An airline spokesperson added: "Our immediate priority is to ensure the ongoing safety, health, and wellbeing of all passengers and crew members involved in this incident and support the official investigation."

The passengers who had been on board flight FZ1073 arrived in Tel Aviv at around 18:40 local time (15:40 GMT). They were greeted at the airport by crowds of onlookers playing music, singing, dancing and waving Israeli flags.
A number of people were "very emotional and crying as they came off the plane," a paramedic from Israel's ambulance service told the BBC.
One passenger, Yaniv Hayun, met Netanyahu and told him how he and others on the flight had restrained the attacker.

"The pilot who was stabbed was simply very close to the door, so it was hard for us to open it," Hayun said in a video posted on social media by the prime minister's office, but before the stabbed pilot - now identified as Machchhar - collapsed, he was able to open the door.
Yaniv said he put the attacker, who was trying to disable the plane, in a chokehold before other passengers helped pin him down.
He added that he "pulled the controls" of the plane and after it levelled out, another pilot took over control.
Zvika Meness, another passenger, told Israeli public broadcaster Kan News that he and other passengers tied the attacker up "with his own zip ties and with the multimedia headphones".
He said: "There are children and families here who have been through a very severe, highly traumatic event."

articles.title: US military cuts generals, admirals by 20%, Hegseth says
articles.summary: The US defense secretary has also unveiled major changes, including a new drone command and an Elon Musk-led task force to assess the future of warfare.

image.caption: 'The pace of war is changing faster than the process to support it,' Hegseth said [FILE: July 27, 2026]Image: Evelyn Hockstein/REUTERS

blocks.text: US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced Wednesday that the United States military has slashed the number of its generals and admirals by 20%.
He made the announcement while addressing junior officers and enlisted leaders at the Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia during what he called his "State of the Force" address.
"The number-crunchers say we fired 10% of the generals and admirals across the force," Hegseth said, adding: "We've also reduced the overall number of general officer slots by an additional 10%."
"So yes, 20% reduction across the board," he noted. "The media calls that a purge. I call it accountability, and long overdue."
How the US is merging artificial intelligence and warfare
Cutting the fat or a purge?
The address came a year after a similar speech to top officers in which Hegseth said the US military was too fat, too focused on leftist "woke" ideas, and in need of major shake-up.
Since the start of Donald Trump's second term as president early last year, a number of top military personnel have been forced out of their positions.
Trump, for instance, fired the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, General Charles "CQ" Brown, without explanation in February 2025.

Other senior officers pushed out include the heads of the US Army, Navy and Coast Guard, the general who headed the National Security Agency, the vice chief of staff of the US Air Force, and a Navy admiral assigned to NATO.
Hegseth has insisted the president is simply choosing the military leaders he wants.
But Democratic lawmakers have raised concerns about the potential politicization of the US military.
Some members of Congress have called the latest cuts to the general ranks a "purge" that will take years to rebuild.

"He's got some kind of like deep-seated grievance about leadership in the military,” Democratic Senator Mark Kelly told the Associated Press. Kelly is a former Navy combat pilot who has been critical of Hegseth. "He's purging a generation of great leaders of the military, and it's going to take a generation to recover from it."
Republican Senator Mike Rounds, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said he wanted to understand Hegseth's reasoning.
"If it's simply a matter of eliminating a very heavy top, there may be some validity to it, but I want to see it first," Rounds said.
Fighting Iran war, can US military sustain a long conflict?
What Hegseth said about the new command
On Wednesday, Hegseth also announced his intention to create a new drone-focused warfare command, which would oversee the rollout of autonomous and robotic capabilities.
He said that "the pace of war is changing faster than the process to support it."
The defense secretary pointed to Ukraine's use of drones to combat Russian forces to underscore how warfare and battlefield tactics are changing.
"Ukraine's lesson is not that one type of drone wins wars, but rather the need for a purpose-built system that maximizes the ability to adapt," Hegseth said.

To study the future of warfare, the secretary unveiled a task force led by tech billionaire Elon Musk, former Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich and Palmer Luckey, co-founder of Anduril Industries.

He said the work "will be focused on discovering, developing and fielding the weapons and systems that our children and our grandchildren will need in their lifetimes." The Pentagon chief pointed to the need to dominate "any future battlefield, from under the Earth to beyond the moon."

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.

blocks.text: Law enforcement officials are looking for additional victims after two bodies were found on Tuesday in a remote area of Lancaster, California, a small city about 70 miles north of Los Angeles, the Los Angeles Times reports.

Authorities found the bodies in a shallow grave while they were investigating a missing persons case, according to KTLA. Outside of the sheriff’s department investigating the discovery of the remains as a homicide, little is known about the two people who were found in the shallow grave.
On Wednesday, KTLA’s helicopter captured authorities and staff with the medical examiner’s office digging in new areas near where the bodies were found.

Lancaster is a city of just over 170,000 people, according to the most recent census data. The city is unincorporated and therefore under the jurisdiction of the county sheriff. Like much of the nation, Lancaster has seen a substantial decrease in homicides, with killings declining by 35% between 2024 and 2025, according to the city.

articles.title: Daredevil Jaan Roose prepares to walk slackline high above central Seoul
articles.summary:
Estonian will navigate narrow ribbon, 160 metres long and 120 metres high, near the city’s famous Gwanghwamun palace on Thursday

Estonian aerial athlete Jaan Roose will attempt to cross a…

blocks.text: Estonian aerial athlete Jaan Roose will attempt to cross a 160-metre long highline suspended 120 metres above central Seoul on Thursday.

Roose, a three-time slackline world champion, will step out on to a narrow polyester ribbon between the Koreana hotel and the Dong-A Media Center, near the capital city’s famous Gwanghwamun palace and square.
The 34-year-old has made a name for himself slacklining dramatic urban environments, such as his 185-metre high feat between Qatar’s Iconic Towers.

In 2024, he became the first person to slackline the strait of Messina between mainland Italy and Sicily, completing the 3.6km traverse despite a fall near the end, caught by his safety harness. Earlier this month, he covered 14.7km over 12 hours on a line above the Danube in Bratislava, Slovakia.

Large crowds in Seoul are expected to watch Roose walk the slackline – twice, at 1pm and 4pm local time – if the weather allows. The walk will be postponed if average wind speeds reach 10m/s or gusts hit 15m/s. Today’s forecast is sunny with light breezes.

blocks.caption: A woman in Warsaw, Poland, watches Estonian slackliner Jaan Roose cross a highline suspended above the city in 2026. Photograph: Marek Antoni Iwańczuk/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Roose said a visit in 2022 to South Korea inspired his Gwanghwamun walk.
On that trip, Roose encountered jultagi, Korea’s traditional tightrope walking, which Unesco added to its list of intangible cultural heritage in 2011.
Unlike tightrope walking elsewhere, jultagi is as much comedy as acrobatics. The walker sings, jokes and dances on the rope, trading banter with a clown on the ground as musicians play.

articles.title: California bans child marriage, a practice still legal in 32 US states
articles.summary: Gov Gavin Newsom called it a "long overdue measure to protect young Californians".

blocks.text: Stodden said she would "keep fighting until children are protected from marriage in all 50 states".

She was married to actor Doug Hutchison - known for roles in The Green Mile, A Time to Kill and I Am Sam - in 2011, spurring headlines internationally over the controversy and appearances on several reality programmes in the US, including the VH1 series Couples Therapy.
Other survivors of child marriage also applauded the new law.

"California has sent a clear message to the world today," Brittany Bee, a former child bride, told the BBC. "A message of hope for all children that they may be free from systemic violence. That they may choose their own path."
Bee told the BBC she was wed at the age of 17 to escape an abusive home - only to then be allegedly abused by her adult husband.
"I was just going from one prison to another," she explained. "People have the audacity to tell me that I made a choice - kids, they can't consent."
Bee and other child marriage survivors have been working for years to have child marriages banned in California and across the United States.
About a decade ago, the practice was still allowed across all US state but more and more states have been altering laws. California is the 18th to ban it since 2018.
In the state, there had been no legal age to wed, allowing children to get married as long as their parents consent and a judge signs off on the nuptials.
There was also no mechanism for people under 18 to get divorced and many girls say they were trapped in abusive and predatory relationships.

Unchained At Last, an advocacy group fighting to end child marriage across the US, said about 9,000 girls were wed each year in California and that almost all child marriages involved girls to adult men.
Advocates say that many in the US don't even know that child marriage is legal in so many US states, nor that is has led to allegations of abuse.

Sara Tasneen, who says she was forced to marry a man nearly twice her age when she was 15 years old, told the BBC that it felt "surreal" to finally have the state recognise that child marriage should be banned. She says she started lobbying for this herself in 2017.
She was introduced to her husband the morning of their arranged marriage.
"I was forced to be his wife and that day, my entire life changed," she told the BBC. She became a mother the following year, at the age of 16, and dropped out of school.
"To have seen the arc of this bill come to fruition has been a marathon," Tasneen said. "I'm just grateful that kids cannot get married after January 1, 2027 in California."

articles.title: Swiss glaciers suffer 'disastrous' year of ice loss, threatening water supplies
articles.summary: Scientists say such rapid melting is no longer surprising given the pace of climate change.

blocks.text: Swiss glaciers have suffered a near-record loss of ice in 2026, new data shows, as intense summer heatwaves take their toll on Alpine peaks.
More than 5% of the country's remaining glacier ice has disappeared in the last 12 months, which scientists say is "extraordinary".
They warn that such rapid melting is no longer a surprise given the pace of climate change, but it could threaten water supplies for farming, hydropower and transport in the decades ahead.
The loss of glacier ice can also destabilise mountain slopes and increase the risk of landslides in some places - which can lead to flash flooding in extreme cases, as seen in Nepal in August.
There were multiple factors involved in that event, which was triggered when a large area of bedrock and glacier ice collapsed.
But scientists say long-term glacier thinning and the thawing of frozen ground likely raised the risks.

The notable finding from this latest report is not so much that Swiss glaciers are shrinking - which is to be expected in our warming climate, driven primarily by fossil fuel emissions - but the sheer pace of melting.
Until recently, glaciologists in the Alps considered 2% of ice lost in a single year to be "extreme". This year has seen an estimated 5.5% disappear.
"It's really just disastrous," said Dr Matthias Huss, director of Glacier Monitoring Switzerland, which produced the report.
One of the most ominous findings is what researchers observed at measurement sites at the highest elevations, where temperatures are lowest and glaciers are typically snow-covered.
Even as high as 3,500 metres above sea level, scientists found no snow remaining at the end of summer.

"At some glaciers we've seen four metres of ice loss at the highest point, where they should be covered by several metres of winter snow at this time of the year," said Huss, from Glacier Monitoring Switzerland.
Snow is like glacier food - and under stable conditions some of it would eventually compact into ice.
But if no snow survives the summer, it cannot replace the ice lost to melting at lower, warmer elevations. The glacier will starve, shrink and eventually disappear.
"Glaciers are complex because they gain mass at the top and they flow downstream, so there is a lot of physics," explained Maussion.
"But in its simplest form, what we see right now is that we took an ice cube out of the fridge and it's just melting in front of our eyes."
Scientists say the climate is now too warm for many Alpine glaciers to survive.
Some, like Plattalva in eastern Switzerland, have already disappeared.

articles.title: Palace: Baste Duterte seems ‘unconcerned’ about VP Sara’s GenCorp stake
articles.summary: The Palace spokesperson stressed that public officials should not use the Arias doctrine to protect their own interests or hide potential negligence of their families and allies.

blocks.text: Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte testifies as a hostile witness on the 31st day of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial at the Senate in Pasay City on Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026.
The STAR / Ryan Baldemor

MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang said Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte seems "unconcerned" about Vice President Sara Duterte’s financial interest in GenCorp Industries Inc. following his appearance as a witness in his sister’s impeachment trial.

At a press briefing on Wednesday, September 30, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro declined to make a conclusion as to whether Baste was covering for Duterte after claiming in his testimony that he only learned about GenCorp through the trial.

“Hindi natin masasabi. Hindi natin mabibigyan ng anumang paghuhusga ang kanyang statement. Ang ipinakita lang niya kahapon ay wala siyang alam. Wala siyang alam. Hindi niya inalam at parang wala siyang pakialam,” Castro said.
(We can’t say. We can’t give any judgment on his statement. What he showed yesterday was that he knows nothing. He is clueless. He did not bother to find out and he seems unconcerned.)

Baste appeared in the Senate impeachment court on Tuesday, September 29, to testify on the alleged unexplained wealth of the vice president, particularly on what the prosecutors claim as a conflict of interest involving GenCorp’s contracts with the Davao City government.
He was later declared by the Senate impeachment court as a hostile witness.
The prosecutors’ arguments stemmed from the P34.2 million worth of 15 contracts in Davao City awarded to GenCorp from 2022 to 2026. Baste, on the other hand, claimed there were 19 contracts.
The vice president is listed as a stockholder in GenCorp, which was also declared in her 2024 and 2025 statements of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALN).
Good faith

Castro also said Baste appeared to defend himself after Senator-judge Panfilo “Ping” Lacson brought up the Arias doctrine during the trial, asking the witness if he had been informed by his counsel regarding it.
“Parang lumalabas na pinagtanggol niya ‘yung sarili niya as a mayor. Inangat niya yung sarili niya as a mayor,” Castro said.
(It appears that he is defending himself as a mayor. He held himself in higher regard as a mayor.)

The Arias doctrine was established in a landmark Supreme Court ruling in 1989, which states that heads of offices can rely in good faith on the decisions and signatures of their subordinates when approving routine documents.
Castro noted that the Arias doctrine can only be invoked in an isolated case and cannot be used to cover up repeated anomalies or signs of irregularities that a public official should have noticed.
The Palace spokesperson also stressed that public officials should not use the doctrine to protect their own interests or hide potential negligence of their families and allies.

“Hindi lang ito para kay Mayor Baste Duterte. Sa lahat na po ng pinuno, dapat maging alerto rin kayo. Hindi pwedeng gamitin itong Arias v. Sandiganbayan para lang isagip ang sarili niyo,” Castro said.
(This is not just for Mayor Baste Duterte. To all head officers, you should be alert. The Arias v. Sandiganbayan cannot be invoked to save yourselves.)

articles.title: US Supreme Court allows execution of Christa Pike to go ahead
articles.summary: The death by lethal injection was scheduled to happen earlier on Wednesday before a lower court paused the execution.

blocks.text: The US Supreme Court has cleared the way for Tennessee inmate Christa Pike to be executed, overturning a last-minute reprieve.

The killing by lethal injection was scheduled for Wednesday morning before judges from the Sixth Circuit Appeals court halted the execution. Tennessee's attorney general then immediately requested the Supreme Court to overrule the lower court's stay.
Pike, 50, has been awaiting execution since she was convicted and sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer.
If the execution proceeds, Christa Pike will be the first woman to be executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. It was not immediately clear when the execution would take place.
Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh granted the application to vacate the stay of the execution. No explanation for lifting the stay was provided in the order.
The top court's three liberal justices - Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson - dissented in Wednesday evening's order.
Sotomayor wrote that she dissents because the decision cleared the way for Tennessee to execute Pike before her pending legal challenges to her conviction "can be properly considered".
"Tennessee's desire to expedite Pike's execution by a few days or even weeks cannot outweigh her 'fundamental interest in [her] own life," she said.

The latest ruling from the Supreme Court came just before 18:00 local time, hours before the state's execution order is set to expire at midnight. If time runs out the Tennessee Supreme Court will need to set a new execution date, the Associated Press reports.
In a ruling earlier on Wednesday, judges from the Sixth Circuit Appeals court paused the execution saying they needed more time to consider the arguments in Pike's case.
Pike's lawyers said that for years, the state of Tennessee argued in court that she had lied about being sexually abused as a child.
But at a recent hearing about her execution method, the state said it did not dispute she suffered sexual abuse and rape.

Pike's legal team asked the appeals court to send her motion back to the district court, arguing that if the federal courts based their ruling on the state's earlier claim that she was lying, then the federal review was affected.
Earlier this week, the Supreme Court refused to hear a different appeal from Pike.
Tennessee governor also denied a clemency request this week from the death row inmate.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens.

articles.title: Cornell case spotlights 'confusing' web of systems for reporting campus assaults
articles.summary: Victims often have to navigate both university and local law enforcement processes to find justice.

blocks.text: Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of sexual assault.

When Mary was a first-year college student, she woke up after a fraternity party with bruises and bite marks all over her body. She says it took her a few days to piece together that she had been sexually assaulted while "blacked out", and to find the strength - and the right avenue - to report the assault.
The man she accused was eventually expelled, but police declined to bring charges because they said there was a lack of physical evidence.
Mary - whose name has been changed to protect her identity - says the process of finding some measure of justice was oftentimes confusing and disappointing.

"Even though it was a positive outcome, it was still so emotionally exhausting and draining, because I had to do all of this in tandem with getting used to being a college student for the first time," said Mary. "In many ways, I had to be my own advocate, gathering all my evidence."
The experience with local police, she added, "left me with a deep sense of disappointment in the system".

How both universities and the criminal justice system respond to these types of assaults on college campuses is once again under the spotlight, after a former student at Cornell University filed a civil lawsuit alleging she was raped by several members of a fraternity two years ago, with prosecutors declining at the time to pursue a case.

Mary did not attend Cornell, and her case is not connected with the university. But advocates for survivors of sexual assault say her case, and the Cornell allegations, are emblematic of the larger challenges in responding to sexual assault claims on college campuses specifically.
The confusing web of systems and policies - which varies greatly by college - is one of several reasons why the vast majority of sexual assaults on college campuses, research suggests, go unreported.

"These processes are hard to navigate if you aren't in trauma," said Nancy Chi Cantalupo, an associate professor of law at Wayne State University who has represented victims on college campuses. "If you are in trauma, they're virtually impossible to navigate."

Earlier this month, the former Cornell student known only as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit against the Ivy League university, alleging she was drugged and raped by several men at a fraternity house at the university in 2024.

She also alleged that Cornell failed to protect her or adequately punish the men involved. Jane Doe said she had reported the alleged assault to campus police, who interviewed her, and provided information to the district attorney's office. The prosecutor declined to bring charges at the time, but this week, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten re-opened the case.

Both Cornell and Van Houten have defended their handling of the 2024 case. In a statement, external, the university said it had "conducted an extensive investigation and adjudication over several months and imposed different sanctions based on the findings and circumstances involving each student" in addition to creating a new framework for addressing sexual assault on campus.

Cornell has said it followed the procedures outlined in a federal civil rights law called Title IX. The law mandates that universities follow certain rules about investigating sexual assaults. Cornell said its investigation resulted in the fraternity involved being barred from campus, and that students involved were suspended or expelled.
Typically, after a student reports an assault on campus, the university's Title IX office determines whether the alleged behaviour could constitute a violation of policy.
Eventually, both parties attend a hearing with a panel of faculty members or other mediators to present evidence and testimony in the case before a decision by the school is reached.

One of the biggest challenges sexual assault survivors face is simultaneously navigating the university and the criminal justice system, which "serve different purposes, operate under different rules and timelines, and lead to different outcomes", said Zoey Scheinblum-Brewer, a policy coordinator at the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network, a nonprofit anti-sexual assault organisation.
"Unclear guidance about the options available through these parallel processes can create so much confusion and uncertainty that some students ultimately decide not to report," she said.
Mary said this process at her college was not clear to her when she made the decision to report the assault.
"For me, it would've been nice to know what I was getting into before it all happened. It felt like they were learning the process alongside me," she said of university officials.

While some colleges, like Cornell, have information sharing agreements with local police, Mary was told she had to go to police separately to file a report - a process she found physically exhausting.

Mary's lawyer says there was surveillance footage from the night showing her alleged rapist carrying her "slumped" over, and she had pictures of her bruises and bite marks. But police told Mary they did not have probable cause for an arrest, and that the district attorney wanted to leave it to university administration.
"I was left with this taste that because they knew that the college was 'handling' my investigation, that they could wipe their hands clean of it," she said.
The local police department told the BBC it did not have the details of this particular case. The local district attorney's office did not respond to a request for comment.

University investigations are done behind closed doors, said Helene Weiss, a lawyer who has represented several victims of sexual assault on college campuses. She believes that part of the reason for the secrecy is to protect institutions' reputations.
"The secrecy of the process, it prevents other students from knowing about it. It prevents witnesses from coming forward," she said.
Michael Diamondstein, a Pennsylvania attorney who has represented those accused of sexual misconduct on college campuses, said the secrecy helps protect both the victim and the accused.

"I think when you compare it to what they would face in a courtroom, it's much easier for students and much safer for students. Their name isn't put out there. The news media doesn't get them," he said.

Cornell students have criticised the university's handling of the woman's claims. The Cornell Daily Sun, a student newspaper, published the names of the accused under the headline: "Cornell won't, we will."

In a statement, the college said that federal privacy law "prohibits Cornell from disclosing specific information regarding individual students" so it cannot "make a public statement on any other disciplinary response".

Many advocates say there is merit to universities investigating sexual assault complaints separately from the criminal justice system. Prosecuting sexual assault cases is notoriously difficult - a recent systematic review found that less than 10% of sexual assault cases yielded convictions. In a criminal trial, a prosecutor must convince a jury "beyond reasonable doubt" that the accused is guilty. But in a campus tribunal, the burden of proof is lower.

Under Title IX, the university is also required to offer solutions that local law enforcement cannot, like ensuring a student is not in the same class as their alleged abuser while the investigation is ongoing and offering homework extensions, said Scheinblum-Brewer.
This is one of several reasons why victims and advocates for survivors say there are benefits to having two separate avenues, through the university and the criminal justice system.
For Mary, after her case was dropped by the police, pursuing her assault claim through Title IX became the only way for her alleged rapist to face repercussions: an expulsion from college.
"This was my only avenue to achieve any sort of justice," she said.

articles.title: Man arrested over alleged plot to attack Texas state capitol
articles.summary:
Suspect Benny Caldera Jr held on bond as officials say they received ‘credible’ information about Austin threat

A 40-year-old man was arrested early Wednesday on suspicion of plotting to…

blocks.text: A 40-year-old man was arrested early Wednesday on suspicion of plotting to attack the Texas state capitol, authorities said.
The Texas department of public safety said in a statement that it received “credible information about an individual planning a violent attack” for Thursday in Austin.
The tip came in Tuesday evening, and Swat officers made the arrest at about 3am on Wednesday at a residence in Converse, Texas, near San Antonio.

Benny Caldera Jr was jailed on a $75,000 bond. He could face charges including felony terroristic threat against a public servant, officials said in a statement. Messages were left seeking comment from an attorney listed for Caldera.

Officials did not provide details about the alleged plot, citing the ongoing investigation. Public safety officials notified state lawmakers about the threat and arrest early on Wednesday. The Capitol remained open during regular operating hours.
Texas senate secretary Patsy Spaw said in a notice that there will be increased security at the Capitol during the investigation.
Governor Greg Abbott said the state DPS was assisted by the FBI in making the arrest.
“Texas will NOT tolerate threats of violence against our Capitol,” the governor said in a statement on social media.
